definition: Signed toroidal orientation angle of a poloidal magnetic-field probe coil’s sensitive-axis normal, expressed in rad. In the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame it is obtained as atan2(n_φ, n_R), where n_R and n_φ are the radial and toroidal components of that normal. It is measured from +R toward the normal’s horizontal projection, positive toward increasing φ; zero corresponds to an outward-directed projection in the poloidal plane.
documentation: This scalar describes the orientation of an individual poloidal magnetic-field probe coil, not its toroidal position around the machine or the magnetic field it measures. It specifies the toroidal orientation of the sensitive axis rather than its poloidal tilt, and differs from the corresponding toroidal angle of a toroidal magnetic-field probe by the type of sensor described. The orientation is part of the probe geometry used to relate its measured field component to the local magnetic-field vector; it is not averaged over probes, turns, or field samples.
enclosing_statements: Poloidal field probes Array of poloidal field (Bp) probe sensors, each measuring the local magnetic field at a point in the tokamak. Stores sensor geometry, turn count, bandwidth, and time-resolved voltage and field signals for equilibrium reconstruction.
name: toroidal_angle_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
source_descriptions: Toroidal angle of coil orientation (0 if fully in the poloidal plane)

definition: Major-radius coordinate of the plasma-current centroid, obtained by normalizing the toroidal-current first moment over the poloidal plasma cross-section by total plasma current.
documentation:
The radial coordinate of the current center is the major-radius location of the centroid of the toroidal plasma-current distribution. It identifies a current-weighted position and is distinct from the geometric centroid or the magnetic axis.

The coordinate is defined by the toroidal-current first moment:

$$
R_c = \frac{\displaystyle\int_{D_p} R\,j_\phi\,dS}{I_p}
$$

where $R_c$ is the major-radius coordinate of the current center, $R$ is the major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $j_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the plasma [current density](name:current_density), $dS$ is an element of poloidal cross-sectional area, $D_p$ is the plasma current-carrying poloidal cross-section, and $I_p$ is the total toroidal plasma current, equal to the corresponding integral of $j_\phi$ over $D_p$.

The quantity applies to the full plasma-current distribution and uses a current-weighted first-moment aggregation over the poloidal cross-section. It excludes weighting by particle density, pressure, magnetic-field strength, or geometric area alone; the resulting position is therefore not a generic geometric center.

This quantity is a locus-specific instance of the general [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate), evaluated at the current center. Its vertical counterpart, [vertical coordinate of the current center](name:vertical_coordinate_of_current_center), supplies the corresponding vertical position needed to locate the current centroid in the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
enclosing_statements: Position and vertical velocity of the current centre
0D parameters of the equilibrium
Set of equilibria at various time slices
name: radial_coordinate_of_current_center
source_descriptions: Major radius of the current center, defined as integral over the poloidal cross section of (j_tor*r*dS) / Ip

definition: Geometric rate at which the cumulative volume enclosed by a nested magnetic flux surface changes with its dimensionful toroidal-flux coordinate. It is evaluated at each equilibrium time slice with time and other coordinates held fixed, is positive as enclosed volume grows monotonically outward, and has unit m^2.
documentation:
This quantity is the geometric derivative of the cumulative volume enclosed by a nested magnetic flux surface with respect to the dimensionful toroidal-flux coordinate. It describes how rapidly the enclosed region expands as the flux-surface label changes.

The defining relation is

$$
\frac{dV}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}}
$$

where $V$ is the [volume enclosed by a flux surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface) and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the dimensionful toroidal-flux coordinate labeling the nested surfaces.

The quantity applies to the three-dimensional region inside each selected nested magnetic flux surface. The volume is cumulative, beginning at the magnetic axis and extending to the specified surface; this is not a local plasma-population quantity and carries no species weighting. It is the derivative with respect to the toroidal-flux coordinate, not the volume itself or the derivative of the enclosed poloidal area. It is evaluated at each equilibrium time slice with time and other coordinates held fixed and is positive as enclosed volume grows monotonically outward.

As the derivative of [volume enclosed by a flux surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface), it provides the volume increment associated with a change in toroidal-flux coordinate and serves as a geometric coefficient in flux-surface-averaged transport relations. The derivative of area with respect to the toroidal-flux coordinate is the analogous area derivative, while [the temporal derivative of this volume derivative](name:time_derivative_of_derivative_of_volume_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate) describes its change in time.
enclosing_statements: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux
Set of equilibria at various time slices

source_descriptions: Radial derivative of the volume enclosed in the flux surface with respect to Rho_Tor

definition: Back-surface neutron energy flux is the local rate of neutron kinetic-energy transfer outward through an object's designated rear surface, per unit actual surface area and time. It is a scalar energy flux, not a neutron count flux, integrated power, or spatial maximum.
documentation:
Backa-surface neutron energy flux is the local rate at which neutron kinetic energy crosses outward through an object's designated rear surface, per unit actual surface area and time. It is a scalar measure of energy transfer, not a neutron count rate.

The local energy flux is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{n,\mathrm{back}}^{E}(\mathbf r,t) = \frac{\partial^2 E_{n,\mathrm{out}}}{\partial A\,\partial t}(\mathbf r,t)
$$

where $\Gamma_{n,\mathrm{back}}^{E}$ is the back-surface neutron energy flux, $n$ identifies the neutron contributions, $\mathbf r$ is position on the back surface, $t$ is time, $E_{n,\mathrm{out}}$ is the cumulative kinetic energy carried by neutrons crossing outward through the surface, and $A$ is actual surface area.

The quantity applies locally over the object's designated back surface and aggregates the kinetic-energy contributions of outward-crossing neutrons across their energies. It excludes neutron number flux, neutron production within a volume, energy deposited inside material, power integrated over a surface, and a spatial maximum or average over the surface.

Integrating the local flux over a portion of the back surface gives the neutron power crossing outward through that portion. The [maximum of back-surface neutron flux](name:maximum_of_back_surface_neutron_flux) is the greatest local value over the applicable back surface; that maximum is not part of this local quantity.
name: back_surface_neutron_energy_flux

definition: Full thickness of a rectangular plasma filament cross-section, measured along the in-plane direction normal to the filament's central segment. It is the transverse side length of the rectangle, complementing the tangential length measured along the segment. The local plane is a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The thickness is a non-negative length in m.
documentation:
Thickness of a plasma filament is the full transverse extent of a rectangular (thick-line) filament cross-section, measured in the local plane of the element along the direction normal to the filament's central segment. The central segment lies in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and the local tangential-normal basis is defined within that plane: the tangential direction follows the central segment while the normal direction is the in-plane perpendicular. It is a full side length, not a half-width.

For a rectangular filament cross-section, the cross-sectional area is the product of the two full local side lengths:

$$
A_\mathrm{fil} = L_\mathrm{tan}\, t
$$

where $A_\mathrm{fil}$ is the filament cross-sectional area in $\mathrm{m}^2$, $L_\mathrm{tan}$ is the tangential length in $\mathrm{m}$, and $t$ is the thickness in $\mathrm{m}$. When the local tangential and normal directions align with the cylindrical axes, the thickness coincides with either the width (radial $R$-direction extent) or the [height](name:height_of_plasma_filament) (vertical $Z$-direction extent) of the same rectangular cross-section.

In equilibrium filament descriptions, the thickness is set by the chosen local geometric representation of a discrete current-carrying plasma element. For a thick-line element it is specified directly as the rectangle side perpendicular to the central segment.

The value is a non-negative geometric length governed by the spatial resolution and local size of the filament representation. No universal device-independent numerical range applies; it should be interpreted relative to the associated tangential length and to neighboring filament spacing.
enclosing_statements: The element is approximated by a rectangle defined by a central segment and a thickness in the direction perpendicular to the segment
Cross-sectional shape of the element

Each element holds a cross-sectional area and time-resolved current, enabling the plasma to be modelled as a distributed current source for electromagnetic circuit and equilibrium calculations.
name: thickness_of_plasma_filament
source_descriptions: Thickness

definition: Faraday angle is the signed rotation of a probing beam's linear-polarization orientation accumulated as the beam propagates through magnetized plasma. It is sensitive to the line integral of electron density times the magnetic-field component along the beam path and is used to constrain equilibrium reconstruction. It is a time-resolved scalar for one polarimeter channel (line of sight), evaluated relative to the beam's initial polarization orientation at its probing wavelength and expressed in rad. It may be measured directly or calculated from the reconstructed equilibrium at the selected time slice.
documentation:
Faraday angle is the signed rotation of the linear-polarization orientation of a probing electromagnetic wave induced by its passage through magnetized plasma. It is the variation of the polarization orientation accumulated between the beam's entry into and exit from the plasma.

In the cold, weakly dispersive magnetoionic limit, the plasma-induced rotation is approximated by

$$
\alpha = \frac{e^3\lambda^2}{8\pi^2\epsilon_0 m_e^2 c^3} \int_{\mathcal{L}} n_e(\ell) B_{\parallel}(\ell)\,d\ell
$$

where $\alpha$ is the Faraday angle, $e$ is the elementary-charge magnitude, $\lambda$ is the vacuum probing wavelength, $\pi$ is the circle constant, $\epsilon_0$ is the vacuum permittivity, $m_e$ is the electron mass, and $c$ is the speed of light. The path $\mathcal{L}$ is the segment of the probing beam crossing the plasma, $\ell$ is position along that path, $n_e(\ell)$ is the local [electron number density](name:electron_density), and $B_{\parallel}(\ell)$ is the signed magnetic-field component along the beam-propagation direction.

The quantity is the electron contribution accumulated along one probing-beam path through the plasma: its aggregation is a line integral along that path, not a local rotation rate, a flux-surface average, or an average or sum over beam paths. Rotation produced outside the plasma, including by optical or calibration elements, is excluded. The same physical angle may be realized either as a direct polarimetric observation or as the value calculated from a reconstructed equilibrium state along the same beam path; both denote this quantity, and their difference is a fit residual rather than another definition of it.

Faraday angle describes rotation of the polarization plane, whereas [polarization ellipticity of a polarimeter beam](name:polarization_ellipticity_of_polarimeter_beam) describes the shape of the polarization ellipse through its axis ratio; the two quantities are distinct and not interchangeable.

Sign convention: Positive when the polarization plane rotates according to the right-hand rule about the beam-propagation direction from its incident reference orientation.
enclosing_statements: Set of faraday angles Set of Faraday angle measurements used as constraints in equilibrium reconstruction. Each entry stores measured, reconstructed, and residual values for the polarimetric rotation angle of a laser beam passing through magnetized plasma.

In case of equilibrium reconstruction under constraints, measurements used to constrain the equilibrium, reconstructed values and accuracy of the fit. The names of the child nodes correspond to the following definition: the solver aims at minimizing a cost function defined as : J=1/2*sum_i [ weight_i^2 (reconstructed_i - measured_i)^2 / sigma_i^2 ]. in which sigma_i is the standard deviation of the measurement error (to be found in the IDS of the measurement)
Set of equilibria at various time slices

Set of channels (lines-of-sight) Array of measurement channels (lines of sight) in a polarimeter diagnostic, each recording the initial polarization state, probing wavelength, and time-resolved Faraday rotation angle and ellipticity induced by the magnetized plasma.
name: faraday_angle
source_descriptions: Measured value

definition: Detected photoelectron rate assigned to each wavelength pixel of a spectrometer channel after electronic gain compensation and relative calibration, but before absolute radiometric calibration.
documentation:
This quantity is the spectrally resolved detection rate of photoelectrons produced by a spectrometer channel. It represents the channel response at an individual wavelength pixel rather than an absolutely calibrated optical emission quantity.

The rate for wavelength pixel $p$ is defined by

$$
R_p = \frac{dN_{\mathrm{pe},p}}{dt}
$$

where $R_p$ is the detected photoelectron rate for pixel $p$, $N_{\mathrm{pe},p}$ is the detected photoelectron count assigned to that pixel, and $t$ is time.

The quantity applies separately to each wavelength pixel of the spectrometer channel, with electronic gain compensation and relative channel calibration applied. It is not summed over the spectral range, and it is not an absolute radiance or photon-flux measurement.

Summing the rates over pixels that contain an identified spectral feature produces the corresponding line-integrated signal, represented by [intensity at spectral line](name:intensity_at_spectral_line). The electrical output [voltage of spectrometer channel](name:voltage_of_spectrometer_channel) is a distinct signal quantity and is not this photoelectron rate.

definition: Volume enclosed by a magnetic flux surface, accumulated over its full interior rather than only the shell between adjacent surfaces. It is evaluated at the selected time slice and expressed in m^3. Each value is a scalar; source representations include a zero-dimensional total plasma volume when the selected surface is the plasma boundary, one-dimensional radial-grid values (as a function of poloidal flux in equilibrium profiles), and two-dimensional values on a grid in a poloidal cross-section. Where profiles are specified on the outboard equatorial mid-plane, grid positions there identify the selected magnetic surfaces; the volume still covers each surface's full interior.
documentation:
Volume of flux surface

The volume is defined by

$$
V = \int_{\Omega} d^3\mathbf{x}
$$

where $V$ is the enclosed volume, $\Omega$ is the spatial domain inside the selected magnetic flux surface, $\mathbf{x}$ is spatial position, and $d^3\mathbf{x}$ is the differential volume element.

The integral covers the entire enclosed region and excludes space outside the selected surface. It is not a local shell volume; differences between enclosed volumes give the volume between neighboring surfaces. For successively enclosing nested surfaces, the volume increases from zero at the magnetic axis.

When the selected surface coincides with the plasma boundary, this quantity equals the [volume enclosed by the plasma boundary](name:volume_of_plasma_boundary). The [poloidal-flux derivative](name:derivative_of_volume_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate) and [toroidal-flux derivative](name:derivative_of_volume_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate) describe its rate of change with their respective flux coordinates and provide the geometric measures relating flux-coordinate intervals to enclosed shell volumes.

A surface formed by points sharing the same magnetic-flux label in a nested-flux-surface configuration. Where $\psi(R, Z) = \mathrm{const}$, $\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux.

This formulation remains valid when changing simultaneously rho_tor_norm into rho_tor in the gradient terms and in the derivatives denoted by the prime. Note that the energy flux includes the energy transported by the particle flux, in this form: Q = V' [- n D (T)' <|grad(rho_tor_norm)|^2> + v (nT) <|grad(rho_tor_norm)|>] + flux_multiplier * T * particle_flux. definition: Non-negative curvature radius (in m) of one arc-of-circle segment used to approximate the cross-sectional contour of a poloidal field coil. The contour lies in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height.
documentation:
Radius of a poloidal-field-coil arc is the non-negative circle radius of a single circular segment of the coil cross-sectional contour, taken in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. The conductor or winding-pack boundary is approximated by connected circular arcs, and this quantity sets the local radius of curvature of one such arc.

For a circular contour segment, the curvature radius $\rho$ (in m) is the inverse magnitude of the planar curvature $\kappa$ (in m$^{-1}$) of the boundary curve in the $(R, Z)$ cross-section:

$$
\rho = \frac{1}{|\kappa|}
$$

where a finite physical arc has $\rho > 0$, and as $\rho$ grows the segment approaches a straight line ($\kappa \to 0$). Each arc is anchored by a start point in the poloidal plane: its major-radius coordinate is given by major_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil and its vertical coordinate by [height_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil); both together with $\rho$ are needed to locate and shape one arc, with the end of each arc coinciding with the start of the next.

The value is determined from the designed circular-arc contour, from CAD geometry, or by fitting circular arcs to surveyed boundary points. Small radii represent tightly rounded corners and compact winding-pack features, while larger radii represent gently curved coil sides; the magnitude scales with coil aperture, winding-pack dimensions, and mechanical-clearance requirements. An analogous arc-of-circle convention applies to iron core segment boundaries via radius_of_iron_core_segment.
name: radius_of_curvature_of_poloidal_field_coil

definition: Toroidal angle locating each point of a control surface about the machine symmetry axis, measured in the right-handed cylindrical frame from the facility-defined zero direction. At each time slice, the angles form a one-dimensional array indexed from 1 to N on which the Fourier decomposition of the normal components of the magnetic field is carried out. The unit is rad.
documentation:
The toroidal angle identifies the azimuthal location of a point on the control surface about the machine symmetry axis. It is the geometrical coordinate defined for [toroidal angle](name:toroidal_angle), with the control-surface locus providing the points to which it applies.

For a point with Cartesian coordinates $x$ and $y$ in the right-handed $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis, the angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame is defined by:

$$
\phi = \operatorname{atan2}(y,x) \pmod{2\pi}
$$

where $R$ is the major radius, $Z$ is vertical height, and the zero of $\phi$ follows the facility-defined reference direction. The angle is periodic, so values differing by an integer multiple of $2\pi$ represent the same toroidal direction; it is distinct from the vertical coordinate of the control surface.

Sign convention: Positive when $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above the $+\hat{Z}$ direction.

definition: Electromotive-force contribution to the plasma loop voltage caused by changing externally generated poloidal magnetic flux, including flux linked through active coils and passive conducting structures. This global, zero-dimensional scalar is V_ext(t) = -dΦ_ext(t)/dt, where Φ_ext(t) is the externally generated poloidal magnetic flux linked by the considered toroidal plasma circuit and t is time; its unit is V. It excludes resistive voltage drops and other non-inductive contributions. Positive when the induced electromotive force has a positive line integral in the direction of increasing toroidal angle φ in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
This quantity is the inductive electromotive-force contribution to the plasma loop voltage produced by time-varying poloidal magnetic flux generated by active coil circuits and magnetically coupled passive conducting structures. It excludes resistive voltage drops and other non-inductive contributions.

The contribution is defined by Faraday's law:

$$
V_{\mathrm{ext}}(t) = -\frac{d\Phi_{\mathrm{ext}}(t)}{dt}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is the externally generated poloidal magnetic flux linked by the considered toroidal plasma circuit and $t$ is time. It contributes to the total [loop voltage at the plasma boundary](name:loop_voltage_at_plasma_boundary); currents in passive conductors are represented by the linked-flux response of structures such as those described by [current of passive structure](name:current_of_passive_structure).

Sign convention: Positive when the induced electromotive force has a positive line integral in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
name: external_loop_voltage

definition: Dimensionless Luce (2013) squareness coefficient for the lower-inner, high-field-side quadrant of a nested magnetic flux surface, measuring signed departure from a reference ellipse.
documentation:
The lower-inner squareness of a flux surface is the dimensionless Luce (2013) shape coefficient that characterizes how the lower, high-field-side quadrant of a nested toroidal magnetic flux surface departs from a reference ellipse sharing the same center, horizontal half-width, and [elongation](name:elongation_of_flux_surface). It is the lower-quadrant component of [inner squareness of a flux surface](name:inner_squareness_of_flux_surface), complementary to [upper-inner squareness of a flux surface](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface).

The reference ellipse is parameterized in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame by

$$
\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{ref}}(\theta)=\left(R_0+a\cos\theta,\;Z_0+\kappa a\sin\theta\right)
$$

where $R$ is major radius, $Z$ is vertical height, $\theta$ is a poloidal parameter, $(R_0,Z_0)$ is the ellipse center, $a$ is its horizontal half-width, and $\kappa$ is its elongation. Within the Luce model, $\zeta_{\mathrm{li}}=0$ represents no additional lower-inner corner shaping; positive values indicate an outward, boxier corner and negative values an inward, more indented corner.

This coefficient describes only the lower high-field-side quadrant and is not an average of the upper and lower inner coefficients.
enclosing_statements: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux
Set of equilibria at various time slices
name: lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface
source_descriptions: Lower inner squareness (definition from T. Luce, Plasma Phys. Control. Fusion 55 (2013) 095009)

definition: Lower operational bound on the pressure-volume throughput delivered by a gas injection valve: the smallest gas throughput the valve can reliably deliver. Throughput is Q_g = p_g dV_g/dt, where p_g is the gas pressure at the flow boundary and dV_g/dt is the volumetric flow rate across that boundary. The quantity is expressed in Pa.m^3.s^-1.
documentation: This scalar specifies the minimum operating throughput of a valve connecting a gas bottle to pipes. It describes the aggregate gas stream, rather than an individual molecular species, mass flow, or particle-number rate. Unlike gas_flow or gas_flow_of_valve, it specifies a lower operational limit rather than an unrestricted delivered throughput; maximum_gas_flow specifies the corresponding upper limit. The source provides the valve's minimum flow rate but does not specify a measurement or calibration procedure.
enclosing_statements: Set of valves connecting a gas bottle to pipes
name: lower_bound_gas_flow
source_descriptions: Minimum flow rate of the valve

definition: Toroidal magnetic field at the magnetic axis is the signed component of the total equilibrium magnetic field in the toroidal direction, including external-coil and plasma-current contributions.
documentation:
Toroidal magnetic field at the magnetic axis is the signed toroidal projection of the total equilibrium [magnetic field](name:magnetic_field). It is evaluated locally at the magnetic axis.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the defining projection is:

$$
B_{\phi,\mathrm{axis}} = \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{axis}} \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}
$$

where $B_{\phi,\mathrm{axis}}$ is the toroidal magnetic field at the magnetic axis, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the total equilibrium magnetic-field vector at that locus, and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle.

The total field includes externally applied and plasma-current-generated contributions. The corresponding projection of the [vacuum magnetic field](name:vacuum_magnetic_field) excludes plasma-current contributions and is therefore a distinct quantity. This on-axis value is neither a magnetic-field magnitude nor a flux-surface average.

Sign convention: Positive when the magnetic field at the magnetic axis projects in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, counterclockwise when viewed from above.

The closed magnetic-field line about which nested toroidal magnetic flux surfaces are arranged. Where $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{p}}(R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}}) = 0$, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{p}}$ is poloidal magnetic field; $R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the O-point inside the nested closed flux surfaces.

definition: Signed azimuthal orientation angle of a poloidal magnetic-field probe’s sensitive-axis normal in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
This quantity is the signed toroidal orientation of the sensitive-axis normal of a poloidal magnetic-field probe coil. It measures the normal’s departure from the poloidal plane through the orientation of its horizontal projection.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the angle is defined by

$$
\alpha_{\mathrm{tor}} = \operatorname{atan2}(n_\phi,n_R), \qquad n_R=\mathbf{n}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{R}}, \quad n_\phi=\mathbf{n}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}
$$

where $\alpha_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal orientation angle, $\mathbf{n}$ is the probe’s sensitive-axis unit normal, $n_R$ and $n_\phi$ are its cylindrical radial and toroidal components, and $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ are the radial and toroidal unit vectors. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the signed angle from the positive radial direction to the horizontal projection of $\mathbf{n}$.

The quantity applies to the geometric orientation of each poloidal magnetic-field probe coil. It is not the local plasma magnetic field, a field component, or an angle averaged over probes, turns, or field samples. The angle determines how the probe’s sensitive direction is related to the local magnetic-field vector and therefore how the measured component is projected. The corresponding toroidal orientation for a toroidal probe is defined by [toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), while its independent poloidal tilt is represented by [poloidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:poloidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe).

Sign convention: Positive when rotation from the positive radial direction toward the horizontal projection of the sensitive-axis normal is toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

definition: Dimensionless signed safety factor q at the magnetic axis, obtained as q_axis = lim(rho→0) q(rho), where rho labels nested closed magnetic flux surfaces and vanishes at the axis. On neighboring surfaces, q is the number of toroidal field-line turns per complete poloidal circuit: q = (1/(2π)) ∮ (B·∇φ)/(B·∇θ) dθ, with B the magnetic field, φ the toroidal angle and θ the poloidal angle. The integral covers one poloidal circuit in axisymmetry or straight-field-line flux coordinates. The toroidal angle is measured in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, increasing counterclockwise when viewed from above; q is positive when φ advances as θ increases. The axis value is a limit, not a direct evaluation of the poloidal-angle integral at the axis. Unit: 1.
documentation: The magnetic axis is the closed magnetic-field line about which nested toroidal magnetic flux surfaces are arranged; in an axisymmetric equilibrium it passes through the O-point where the poloidal magnetic field vanishes. This quantity specifies the safety factor at that locus, rather than on an unspecified flux surface, at the pedestal, at an internal transport barrier or at the plasma boundary. It is neither a spatial average nor the minimum safety factor over the equilibrium domain, which need not occur at the axis. It is also distinct from magnetic shear at the axis, which describes variation of the safety factor rather than its value.

definition: Outer radius of a plasma filament is the geometric radius of the outer circular boundary of the annular cross-section representing a current-carrying plasma filament. It marks the external boundary of the conducting annular region. In the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, it is the nonnegative distance r_outer = sqrt((R - R_c)^2 + (Z - Z_c)^2), where R is major radius, φ is toroidal angle, Z is vertical height, (R_c, Z_c) is the cross-section center, and (R, Z) is any point on the outer circular boundary. It is a single geometric radius for that boundary, not an average over the conducting region, and is expressed in metres (m).
documentation:
Outer radius of a plasma filament is the geometric radius of the outer circular boundary of the annular cross-section representing a current-carrying plasma filament. It marks the external boundary of the conducting annular region; material outside this boundary is not part of that annular filament cross-section.

For the outer circular boundary in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the outer radius $r_\mathrm{outer}$ is the distance from the filament cross-section center $(R_c, Z_c)$ to any point $(R, Z)$ on that boundary:

$$
r_\mathrm{outer} = \sqrt{(R - R_c)^2 + (Z - Z_c)^2}
$$

where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical height, $(R_c, Z_c)$ is the center of the annular cross-section, and $(R, Z)$ lies on the outer circular boundary.

The quantity applies only to the outer boundary of an annular plasma-filament cross-section and is a single geometric radius for that boundary, not an average over the conducting region. It is the outer member of radius of a plasma filament, paired with the [inner radius](name:inner_radius_of_plasma_filament) $r_\mathrm{inner}$; by definition $0 \le r_\mathrm{inner} \le r_\mathrm{outer}$, and the current-carrying cross-section occupies the annular region between the two radii. For the same annular geometry, the area of a plasma filament $A$ satisfies $A = \pi(r_\mathrm{outer}^2 - r_\mathrm{inner}^2)$, where $A$ is the area of the annular plasma-filament cross-section and $\pi$ is the circle constant. This quantity excludes the major radius of the filament center about the toroidal symmetry axis and rectangular cross-section dimensions such as [plasma filament width](name:plasma_filament_width) and [height of a plasma filament](name:height_of_plasma_filament).
name: outer_radius_of_plasma_filament

The reference point is the annulus centre or the first or second endpoint of the central segment defining a thick-line geometry, as specified by the source.
documentation: This scalar locates a reference point in the cross-sectional geometry of an active poloidal-field coil, including central-solenoid and shaping coils. For an annular geometry it locates the annulus centre; for a thick-line geometry it locates one endpoint of the central segment used with a perpendicular thickness to define the rectangular approximation. It is not necessarily the coil centre, an average over the coil, or the inner or outer radius measured from an annulus centre. Unlike the radial outline of a poloidal-field coil, it does not describe the complete cross-sectional boundary; its locus is the poloidal-field coil rather than a separately identified conductor cross-section or coil-conductor element.

definition: Poloidal arc length of a closed magnetic-flux-surface contour in an equilibrium poloidal cross-section, measuring the perimeter of that selected surface.
documentation:
The poloidal length is the perimeter of the closed contour formed by one selected magnetic flux surface in a poloidal cross-section. It is a geometric property of the surface boundary, rather than its enclosed area, volume, or toroidal circumference.

The contour length is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height:

$$
L_{\mathrm{pol}} = \int_{\theta_a}^{\theta_b} \sqrt{\left(\frac{dR(\theta)}{d\theta}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{dZ(\theta)}{d\theta}\right)^2}\,d\theta
$$

Here $L_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the poloidal length, $\theta$ is any smooth parameter along the contour, $R(\theta)$ and $Z(\theta)$ are its cylindrical coordinate functions, and $\theta_a$ and $\theta_b$ are parameter values at the same contour point after one complete circuit. The contour is taken at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$.

The quantity applies to one magnetic flux surface and includes the complete closed poloidal contour, with no averaging or summation over multiple surfaces. It excludes local arc segments and geometric quantities associated with the enclosed region. The selected surface may be labeled by the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate).

Unlike [elongation of a flux surface](name:elongation_of_flux_surface), which describes a scale-independent cross-sectional shape ratio, the poloidal length retains the absolute geometric scale of the contour.

definition: Dimensionless minor-radius label of a magnetic flux surface, obtained by normalizing its major-radius half-width in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame to a specified positive reference length.
documentation:
This quantity is the dimensionless minor-radius label assigned to a magnetic flux surface from its radial extent in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{minor}} = \frac{R_{\max}-R_{\min}}{2L_{\mathrm{ref}}}
$$

where $R_{\max}$ and $R_{\min}$ are the maximum and minimum major-radius coordinates of the surface, each in m, and $L_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the specified positive reference length in m.

The label is a geometric normalization of the surface half-width; it is not a magnetic-flux normalization and therefore is distinct from the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate). Its numerical value depends on the chosen reference length.

definition: Non-negative curvature radius, in m, of one arc-of-circle segment used to approximate the cross-sectional contour of a poloidal field coil. The contour lies in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height.
documentation:
Radius of a poloidal-field-coil arc is the non-negative circle radius of a single circular segment of the coil cross-sectional contour, taken in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. The conductor or winding-pack boundary is approximated by connected circular arcs, and this quantity sets the local radius of curvature of one such arc.

For a circular contour segment, the curvature radius $\rho$ (in m) is the inverse magnitude of the planar curvature $\kappa$ (in m$^{-1}$) of the boundary curve in the $(R, Z)$ cross-section:

$$
\rho = \frac{1}{|\kappa|}
$$

where a finite physical arc has $\rho > 0$, and as $\rho$ grows the segment approaches a straight line ($\kappa \to 0$). Each arc is anchored by a start point in the poloidal plane: its major-radius coordinate is given by major_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil and its vertical coordinate by [height_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil); both together with $\rho$ are needed to locate and shape one arc, with the end of each arc coinciding with the start of the next.

The value is determined from the designed circular-arc contour, from CAD geometry, or by fitting circular arcs to surveyed boundary points. Small radii represent tightly rounded corners and compact winding-pack features, while larger radii represent gently curved coil sides; the magnitude scales with coil aperture, winding-pack dimensions, and mechanical-clearance requirements. An analogous arc-of-circle convention applies to iron core segment boundaries via radius_of_iron_core_segment.
name: curvature_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil

definition: Ratio of the squared gradient magnitude of the length-valued toroidal-flux coordinate to squared major radius, defining a local equilibrium metric coefficient. It is obtained pointwise as G = |∇ρ_tor|²/R², using the Euclidean norm of the spatial gradient, without spatial averaging. The length-valued coordinate ρ_tor retains its prescribed scale, with no boundary normalization or substitution of an arbitrary flux label. In the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, R is the distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, φ is the toroidal angle, and Z is the vertical height. The denominator is R², not its inverse. The unit is m^-2.
documentation:
Ratio of the squared toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient magnitude to squared major radius is a local equilibrium metric coefficient. It encodes flux-surface spacing with inverse-square major-radius weighting.

The defining relation is:

$$
G = \frac{|\nabla \rho_{\mathrm{tor}}|^2}{R^2}
$$

where $G$ is this local coefficient, $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the length-valued toroidal-flux coordinate, and $\nabla$ is the spatial gradient operator. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is the distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the vertical height.

The toroidal-flux coordinate retains its prescribed scale; no boundary normalization or substitution of an arbitrary flux label is implied. The denominator is squared major radius, not its inverse. The squared gradient magnitude distinguishes this coefficient from inverse squared major radius alone.

This quantity is a pointwise ratio without spatial averaging. Its flux-surface-averaged counterpart averages the complete ratio over a closed magnetic flux surface; it is not the ratio of separately averaged numerator and denominator.

$$a/b$$

The magnitude is the Euclidean norm of a vector quantity, or the modulus of a complex one.

The ratio is one quantity divided by another.

The square is a scalar quantity multiplied by itself, or a vector's dot product with itself.

definition: Faraday angle is the signed rotation of a probing beam's linear-polarization orientation accumulated as the beam propagates through magnetized plasma. It is sensitive to the line integral of electron density times the magnetic-field component along the beam path and is used to constrain equilibrium reconstruction.
documentation:
Faraday angle is the signed rotation of the linear-polarization orientation of a probing electromagnetic wave induced by its passage through magnetized plasma. It is the variation of the polarization orientation accumulated between the beam's entry into and exit from the plasma.

In the cold, weakly dispersive magnetoionic limit, the plasma-induced rotation is approximated by

$$
\alpha = \frac{e^3\lambda^2}{8\pi^2\epsilon_0 m_e^2 c^3} \int_{\mathcal{L}} n_e(\ell) B_{\parallel}(\ell)\,d\ell
$$

where $\alpha$ is the Faraday angle, $e$ is the elementary-charge magnitude, $\lambda$ is the vacuum probing wavelength, $\pi$ is the circle constant, $\epsilon_0$ is the vacuum permittivity, $m_e$ is the electron mass, and $c$ is the speed of light. The path $\mathcal{L}$ is the segment of the probing beam crossing the plasma, $\ell$ is position along that path, $n_e(\ell)$ is the local [electron number density](name:electron_density), and $B_{\parallel}(\ell)$ is the signed magnetic-field component along the beam-propagation direction.

The quantity is the electron contribution accumulated along one probing-beam path through the plasma: its aggregation is a line integral along that path, not a local rotation rate, a flux-surface average, or an average or sum over beam paths. Rotation produced outside the plasma, including by optical or calibration elements, is excluded. The same physical angle may be realized either as a direct polarimetric observation or as the value calculated from a reconstructed equilibrium state along the same beam path; both denote this quantity, and their difference is a fit residual rather than another definition of it.

Faraday angle describes rotation of the polarization plane, whereas [polarization ellipticity of a polarimeter beam](name:polarization_ellipticity_of_polarimeter_beam) describes the shape of the polarization ellipse through its axis ratio; the two quantities are distinct and not interchangeable.

Sign convention: Positive when the polarization plane rotates according to the right-hand rule about the beam-propagation direction from its incident reference orientation.
enclosing_statements: Set of faraday angles Set of Faraday angle measurements used as constraints in equilibrium reconstruction. Each entry stores measured, reconstructed, and residual values for the polarimetric rotation angle of a laser beam passing through magnetized plasma.

In case of equilibrium reconstruction under constraints, measurements used to constrain the equilibrium, reconstructed values and accuracy of the fit. The names of the child nodes correspond to the following definition: the solver aims at minimizing a cost function defined as : J=1/2*sum_i [ weight_i^2 (reconstructed_i - measured_i)^2 / sigma_i^2 ]. in which sigma_i is the standard deviation of the measurement error (to be found in the IDS of the measurement)

definition: Poloidal magnetic flux is the signed magnetic flux through a horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis, labeling magnetic surfaces in axisymmetric equilibrium. The disk is bounded by the toroidal circle through the evaluation point, with its normal toward increasing Z. In the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, R is major radius, φ increases counterclockwise when viewed from above, and Z is vertical height; at time t, the full flux is ψ(R,Z,t) = 2π ∫₀ᴿ B_Z(R′,Z,t) R′ dR′, in Wb, where B_Z is the vertical magnetic-field component. It includes plasma-current and external-source contributions and is not divided by 2π, normalized, or cross-sectionally averaged. Values are provided for various time slices on one-dimensional radial grids, two-dimensional poloidal-plane grids, or general grid subsets with one scalar value per subset element.
documentation:
Poloidal magnetic flux is the net magnetic flux through a horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis and bounded by the toroidal circle through the evaluation point. It specializes [magnetic flux](name:magnetic_flux) by specifying the integration surface and its orientation. In axisymmetric equilibrium, its level sets define magnetic surfaces.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counterclockwise when viewed from above, and $Z$ is vertical height. The full poloidal magnetic flux is defined by

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{p}}(R,Z) \equiv \psi(R,Z) = 2\pi \int_0^R B_Z(R',Z)\,R'\,dR'
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{p}}$, also denoted $\psi$, is the poloidal magnetic flux, $B_Z$ is the vertical magnetic-field component, and $R'$ is the radial integration variable. The factor $2\pi$ accounts for integration around the complete toroidal circle.

This quantity includes contributions from plasma currents and external sources, unlike [external magnetic flux](name:external_magnetic_flux), which excludes the plasma-generated contribution. It is the full flux, not flux divided by $2\pi$, a normalized coordinate, or a cross-sectional average. It differs from [toroidal magnetic flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux), which integrates the toroidal magnetic field through a poloidal cross-section.

The [magnetic-axis value](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis) and [plasma-boundary value](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary) are evaluations of this same function and provide the endpoint references for poloidal-flux normalization. For nested surfaces enclosing positive toroidal plasma current flowing toward increasing $\phi$, the poloidal flux decreases from the magnetic axis to the plasma boundary.

Sign convention: Positive when the magnetic field threading the horizontal disk has a net component toward increasing $Z$, along the upward surface normal.

definition: Plasma current is the total signed conventional electric current carried toroidally by the entire plasma population through a complete poloidal cross-section. Related specialized quantities retain the signed-current meaning while restricting the population, selecting a current direction, or limiting the enclosed region.
documentation:
Plasma current is the net conventional electric current carried in the toroidal direction by the entire plasma population. It is the signed total through a complete poloidal cross-section, with contributions in opposite directions combined algebraically.

The total plasma current is the toroidal projection of plasma current density integrated over the full plasma cross-section:

$$
I_p = \int_{A_p} \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{pl}} \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}\,\mathrm{d}A
$$

where $I_p$ is plasma current, $A_p$ is the full poloidal cross-sectional area occupied by the plasma, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{pl}}$ is the total plasma [current density](name:current_density), $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is the toroidal unit vector, and $\mathrm{d}A$ is a differential cross-sectional area element. The cross-section is at fixed toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; its positive normal is $+\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$.

The total includes current contributions from all plasma charge carriers over the complete cross-section; it is neither a species-resolved current nor an unsigned particle flow or current-density magnitude. Currents carried by external coils and [passive structures](name:current_of_passive_structure) are excluded. Related specialized plasma-current quantities retain the signed conventional-current meaning while specifying a restricted population, direction, or region.

The [cumulative plasma current inside a magnetic flux surface](name:cumulative_inside_flux_surface_plasma_current) restricts the integrated region to the area enclosed by that surface; its toroidal value at the full plasma boundary recovers this total. The [parallel cumulative plasma current inside a flux surface](name:parallel_cumulative_inside_flux_surface_plasma_current) instead selects the local magnetic-field direction, so it is not generally equal to the toroidal current. The [total toroidal runaway-electron current](name:toroidal_total_runaway_electron_current) is the contribution from the runaway-electron population, not the total current of the plasma.

Sign convention: Positive when conventional plasma current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counterclockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

definition: Total non-inductive power coupled from external neutral-beam and radio-frequency heating systems to the plasma, summed over auxiliary sources and excluding Ohmic heating.
documentation:
Total external heating power is the aggregate non-inductive power coupled to the plasma by auxiliary heating systems. It includes neutral-beam injection and electron-cyclotron, ion-cyclotron, and lower-hybrid systems, while excluding power associated with Ohmic induction.

The defining aggregate relation is

$$
P_{\mathrm{ext}} = \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{aux}}} P_s
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is the total external heating power, $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{aux}}$ is the set of included auxiliary heating systems, and $P_s$ is the power coupled to the plasma by auxiliary source $s$.

The quantity applies to the whole plasma and is summed over all included auxiliary sources rather than resolved by source, species, or spatial region. It represents external power input that may contribute to both plasma heating and non-inductive current drive; it is distinct from Ohmic heating and from generator power that is not coupled to the plasma. Source-specific contributions include [total power due to electron-cyclotron heating](name:total_power_due_to_electron_cyclotron_heating), [total power due to ion-cyclotron heating](name:total_power_due_to_ion_cyclotron_heating), and power absorbed from a neutral-beam injector, whose aggregate forms contribute to the sum.

Represents the total non-inductive auxiliary power input.

definition: Shift of pellet-material deposition relative to its ablation location caused by E×B drift, expressed as a difference in normalized toroidal flux coordinate.
documentation:
The pellet deposition displacement describes the shift of ablated pellet material from its ablation location to its final deposition location attributable to E-cross-B drift. It is expressed as a difference in normalized toroidal flux coordinate.

The displacement is defined by deposition minus ablation:

$$
\Delta\rho_{\mathrm{tor},\mathrm{N}} = \rho_{\mathrm{tor},\mathrm{N},\mathrm{dep}} - \rho_{\mathrm{tor},\mathrm{N},\mathrm{abl}}
$$

where $\Delta\rho_{\mathrm{tor},\mathrm{N}}$ is the pellet deposition displacement, and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor},\mathrm{N},\mathrm{dep}}$ and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor},\mathrm{N},\mathrm{abl}}$ are the normalized toroidal flux coordinates at the final deposition and ablation locations, respectively.

Each value concerns material ablated at the corresponding location along the pellet path, not a path-integrated displacement. Only the shift attributed to E-cross-B drift is included. This coordinate difference is neither an absolute deposition coordinate nor a geometric distance or drift velocity; it describes redistribution of ablated material rather than the injection motion characterized by the [initial pellet velocity](name:initial_velocity_of_pellet).

definition: The externally generated inductive electromotive-force contribution to the plasma loop voltage, in V. It is obtained from Faraday's law as V_ext(t) = -dPhi_ext(t)/dt, where Phi_ext is the poloidal magnetic flux linked by the considered toroidal plasma circuit and generated by active coils and magnetically coupled passive conducting structures. documentation: This scalar describes the external-source contribution rather than the total loop voltage at the plasma boundary; it excludes resistive voltage drops and other non-inductive contributions. definition: Vertical coordinate of a measurement position, specifying its signed location along the vertical direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
The vertical coordinate of a measurement position is its signed coordinate along the vertical direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The vertical direction is parallel to the toroidal symmetry axis.

The coordinate is the projection of the position vector onto the vertical direction:

$$
Z = \mathbf{x}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}}
$$

Here $Z$ is the vertical coordinate, $\mathbf{x}$ is the position vector from the coordinate origin to the measurement position, and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the unit vector along the symmetry axis in the positive vertical direction. In the frame $(R, \phi, Z)$, $R$ is major radius measured from the symmetry axis, and $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counterclockwise when viewed from above the positive vertical direction.

This is one coordinate component of the represented measurement position, not the complete position or a measured physical value. Each value pertains to the position under consideration rather than aggregating coordinates over a population of positions. Its corresponding major-radius component is the [radial coordinate of the measurement position](name:radial_coordinate_of_measurement_position).

Sign convention: Positive when the displacement from the coordinate origin to the measurement position points in the direction of increasing $Z$.

definition: Dimensionless plasma-pressure beta relative to a current-based poloidal magnetic-pressure scale, defined as βp = 4∫V p dV/(R₀ μ₀ Ip²), with unit 1. Here p is the plasma pressure supplied by the source, V is the evaluation volume, R₀ is the reference major radius, μ₀ is vacuum permeability, and Ip is the plasma current used in the normalization. It compares volume-averaged pressure with a poloidal rather than toroidal magnetic-pressure scale.
documentation: The global value integrates pressure over the plasma volume; the radial profile evaluates the pressure content inside the corresponding flux surface. Where pressure is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction, the same normalization applies to that reconstructed pressure. In the canonical relation βp = 2μ₀⟨p⟩V/Bp,ref², the volume average is ⟨p⟩V = (1/V)∫V p dV and the effective reference field satisfies Bp,ref² = μ₀²Ip²R₀/(2V). This is a current-based field scale, not a pointwise poloidal field or an average of local pressure-to-field ratios. Unlike toroidal beta, it uses the poloidal magnetic-pressure scale; unlike pedestal electron beta, it is not restricted to local electron thermal pressure. The normalization requires nonzero plasma current and positive evaluation volume.

definition: Local particle number density of hydrogen ions in the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing limiter surface, evaluated on the plasma side of the magnetic presheath or sheath entrance.
documentation:
Hydrogen density at a limiter is the local number density of hydrogen ions in the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing limiter surface. The evaluation point is on the plasma side of the magnetic presheath or sheath entrance; neutral hydrogen is excluded. For hydrogen, the charge-state sum reduces to the density of positively charged hydrogen ions, H+.

The local hydrogen-ion density is defined from the velocity distribution function:

$$
n_{\mathrm{H}^+} = \int f_{\mathrm{H}^+}(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{H}^+}$ is the hydrogen-ion number density, $f_{\mathrm{H}^+}$ is the hydrogen-ion velocity distribution function, and $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity at the evaluation point.

This quantity is the hydrogen-specific component of [density_at_limiter](name:density_at_limiter). It counts hydrogen ions separately from [deuterium_density_at_limiter](name:deuterium_density_at_limiter), and does not include neutral hydrogen or other ion species.

definition: Geometric rate of change of the cumulative volume enclosed by a nested magnetic flux surface as its signed poloidal flux coordinate varies.
documentation:
This quantity is the geometric derivative of the cumulative volume enclosed by a nested magnetic flux surface with respect to its signed poloidal magnetic-flux coordinate.

It is defined by

$$
\frac{dV}{d\psi}=\frac{d}{d\psi}V(\psi)
$$

where $V(\psi)$ is the volume enclosed by the flux surface labeled by $\psi$, $\psi$ is the signed poloidal magnetic-flux coordinate, and $d/d\psi$ denotes differentiation with respect to that coordinate.

The quantity applies separately to each nested closed flux surface. The underlying volume is cumulative from the magnetic axis to the selected surface, so this derivative describes the change in enclosed volume along the flux coordinate rather than a local volume density, a shell volume, or a plasma-population-weighted quantity.

It is the derivative of [volume enclosed by a flux surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface); integrating it between two flux-coordinate values gives the difference between the corresponding enclosed volumes. It is distinct from the derivative with respect to the toroidal flux coordinate, which is represented by [derivative of volume with respect to toroidal flux coordinate](name:derivative_of_volume_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate).

Sign convention: Positive when the enclosed volume increases in the direction of increasing signed poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$.

definition: Major radius averaged over a complete closed magnetic flux surface gives the mean perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis. At each equilibrium time slice, this scalar coefficient is supplied as a one-dimensional radial profile as a function of poloidal magnetic flux ψ. The normalized average is R̄(ψ) = (∮ R dS/|∇ψ|)/(∮ dS/|∇ψ|), where R is the pointwise major radius, dS is the surface-area element, and ψ labels the surface; thus the weighting is the inverse magnitude of the poloidal flux gradient. The unit is m.
documentation:
Major radius is the [radius](name:radius) measured perpendicular to the toroidal symmetry axis. Its flux-surface-averaged value is a geometric equilibrium coefficient for each complete closed magnetic flux surface of a nested equilibrium.

Its defining operator composition is

$$\langle f\rangle = \oint f\,dS/|\nabla\psi| \,/\, \oint dS/|\nabla\psi|$$

where $\overline{R}(\psi)$ is this coefficient, $R$ is the pointwise [major radius](name:major_radius), $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux labeling the surface, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_\psi$ denotes the flux-surface average on that surface.

This quantity is the averaged counterpart of pointwise major radius, not a volume average or the major radius evaluated at a selected point. It applies wherever the flux-surface average is well defined and finite.

The reciprocal of this mean generally differs from the [flux-surface-averaged inverse of major radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_major_radius), because that sibling applies inversion before averaging.

The flux-surface average is the average of a quantity over a closed magnetic flux surface, weighted by the inverse magnitude of the poloidal flux gradient.

definition: Dimensionless factor controlling the relative contribution of an interferometer beam’s line-integrated electron-density residual to an equilibrium objective function. At each equilibrium time slice, it is the nonnegative scalar w_i assigned to one such measurement constraint in J = (1/2) sum_i [w_i^2 (y_i^rec - y_i^meas)^2 / sigma_i^2], where y_i^rec and y_i^meas are the reconstructed and measured line-integrated electron densities, sigma_i is the standard deviation of the measurement error, and the sum runs over individual constraints. Its unit is 1.
documentation:
The equilibrium weight assigned to an interferometer-beam constraint is a nonnegative factor that sets the relative importance of its line-integrated electron-density residual in an equilibrium objective function. It applies to the constraint associated with one interferometer beam rather than to the electron density itself.

A weighted least-squares objective containing this constraint is defined by

$$
J = \frac{1}{2} \sum_i w_i^2 \left(\frac{y_i^{\mathrm{rec}} - y_i^{\mathrm{meas}}}{\sigma_i}\right)^2
$$

where $J$ is the equilibrium objective function, $i$ indexes individual constraints, $w_i$ is the equilibrium weight, $y_i^{\mathrm{rec}}$ is the reconstructed line-integrated electron density for constraint $i$, $y_i^{\mathrm{meas}}$ is its measured line-integrated electron density, and $\sigma_i$ is the standard deviation assigned to its measurement error.

For this quantity, $i$ denotes an interferometer-beam line-integrated electron-density constraint. The weight is specific to that individual constraint; the objective function aggregates all constraint contributions through the summation. It is not the line-integrated electron density, either its measured or reconstructed value, and it is distinct from the [calibration coefficient of an interferometer beam](name:spectral_calibration_factor_at_line_of_sight), which characterizes signal calibration rather than equilibrium-objective weighting.

This quantity has the same objective-function role as the equilibrium weight of a flux loop and the equilibrium weight of a poloidal magnetic-field probe; those related weights differ by the physical measurement constraint to which they apply.

This coordinate difference is neither an absolute deposition coordinate nor a geometric distance or drift velocity; it describes redistribution of ablated material rather than the injection motion characterized by the [initial pellet velocity](name:initial_velocity_of_pellet).

definition: Elongation of a flux surface is the ratio of its poloidal cross-section’s vertical extent to its radial extent, independent of overall size. In the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius, φ is toroidal angle, and Z is vertical height, it is κ = (Z_max − Z_min)/(R_max − R_min), using the maximum and minimum coordinates of the cross-section. It is dimensionless, with unit 1, and applies to an individual surface of constant magnetic-flux label in a nested-flux-surface configuration, not an average over nested surfaces; where ψ(R, Z) = const, ψ is poloidal magnetic flux. For an elliptical cross-section it equals the ratio of vertical to horizontal semi-axes, but no elliptical shape is required. It is not restricted to the plasma boundary. In equilibrium profiles it is supplied on a one-dimensional radial grid as a function of poloidal flux at each time slice; for a local flux surface it is a scalar.
documentation:
Elongation of flux surface

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the defining relation is:

$$
\kappa = (Z_{\max} - Z_{\min})/(R_{\max} - R_{\min})
$$

where $\kappa$ is the elongation, $Z_{\max}$ and $Z_{\min}$ are the maximum and minimum vertical coordinates of the cross-section, and $R_{\max}$ and $R_{\min}$ are its maximum and minimum major radii.

The quantity applies to an individual flux surface, not an average over nested surfaces. For an elliptical cross-section, it equals the ratio of the vertical to horizontal semi-axes; the extent-based definition does not require an ellipse. It is not restricted to the plasma boundary: evaluating it there gives the [elongation of the plasma boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary).

The [derivative of elongation with respect to normalized minor radius](name:derivative_of_elongation_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_normalized_minor_radius) describes how this ratio changes between neighboring surfaces, rather than the shape ratio itself.

A surface formed by points sharing the same magnetic-flux label in a nested-flux-surface configuration. Where $\psi(R, Z) = \mathrm{const}$, $\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux.

definition: Flux-surface-averaged rate of Coulomb-collisional energy transfer per unit volume from ions of one specified species and charge state to co-passing fast particles. The volume-shell-weighted magnetic flux-surface average is reported as a one-dimensional radial profile or a two-dimensional profile in the poloidal plane for various time slices, in W.m^-3. Each distribution describes only one particle species; multiple fast-particle distributions for the same species are superposed.
documentation: Co-passing fast-particle collisional power density due to a specified ion charge state is the signed volumetric rate of kinetic-energy transfer from ions of one specified species and charge state to the co-passing part of a fast-particle distribution, averaged over a magnetic flux surface. The co-passing restriction selects the receiving particles' passing guiding-center orbits, not the supplying ions' orbit class. The defining kinetic-energy moment is $P_{i,q}^{\mathrm{ion}\to\mathrm{co}} = \left\langle \int \frac{1}{2}m_f v^2 C_f^{\mathrm{coll}}\!\left[f_{\mathrm{co}}^{\mathrm{fast}},f_{i,q}\right] \, d^3v \right\rangle_{\psi}$, where $P_{i,q}^{\mathrm{ion}\to\mathrm{co}}$ is this power density, $i$ identifies the supplying ion species, $q$ is its specified ionic charge number, $m_f$ is the recipient fast-particle mass, $v$ is the recipient speed, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. The distribution $f_{\mathrm{co}}^{\mathrm{fast}}$ describes the recipient co-passing fast particles, while $f_{i,q}$ describes the supplying ions. The operator $C_f^{\mathrm{coll}}$ gives the collisional time derivative of the recipient distribution due to those ions. The brackets denote the volume-shell-weighted magnetic flux-surface average, with $\psi$ labeling the surface. Only the specified supplying species and charge state are included; no supplying-species or charge-state sum is implied. Counter-passing and trapped recipients are excluded. Unlike [co-passing thermal-ion charge-state collisional power density](name:co_passing_thermal_power_density_due_to_coulomb_collisions_with_ion_state), this quantity concerns transfer to fast particles from an ion charge state rather than transfer from fast particles to thermal recipient ions. It is an energy-exchange rate, not stored kinetic-energy density or volume-integrated power. Summing over all ionic charge states of the same supplying species gives the collisional power density transferred from that ion species to co-passing fast particles. Its relationship to the all-orbit quantity is an aggregation over co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped recipients with the same supplying population and transfer direction. Transfer from a fast-particle distribution to an ion charge state is a different exchange and must not be substituted for the ion-to-fast transfer defined here. The quantity is reported as a one-dimensional radial profile or a two-dimensional profile in the poloidal plane for various time slices. Every distribution describes only one particle species; multiple fast-particle distributions for the same species are superposed. Sign convention: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy from the specified ion charge-state population to the co-passing fast-particle distribution; negative when the net transfer is reversed.

definition: Poloidal beta compares volume-averaged plasma pressure with an effective poloidal magnetic-pressure scale set by net plasma current and plasma geometry. It is defined as βp = 4∫_V p dV/(R₀μ₀Ip²), with dimensionless unit 1, where p is the pressure supplied by the plasma or equilibrium representation, R₀ is the reference major radius, μ₀ is vacuum permeability and Ip is the plasma current used by that normalization. The global value uses the plasma volume; the one-dimensional radial profile uses the volume inside each flux surface and is a function of poloidal flux. Equilibrium values are evaluated at each time slice. For the equilibrium-reconstruction estimate, p is the pressure determined by an equilibrium reconstruction code.
documentation: Poloidal beta compares the volume-averaged plasma pressure with a current-based poloidal magnetic-pressure scale. Its source normalization is $\beta_p=4\int_V p\,dV/(R_0\mu_0 I_p^2)$. Here $p$ is the pressure supplied by the plasma or equilibrium representation, $V$ is the evaluation volume, $R_0$ is the reference major radius, $\mu_0$ is vacuum permeability and $I_p$ is the plasma current used by that normalization. The global value uses the plasma volume; a radial profile uses the volume inside each flux surface as a function of poloidal flux. Equilibrium values are evaluated at each time slice; the equilibrium-reconstruction estimate uses pressure determined by an equilibrium reconstruction code. Writing $\langle p\rangle_V=V^{-1}\int_Vp\,dV$, the same quantity obeys the canonical beta relation $$\beta = \frac{2\mu_0 \langle p\rangle}{B^2}$$ with $\beta=\beta_p$, $\langle p\rangle=\langle p\rangle_V$ and $B=B_{p,\mathrm{ref}}$. The effective reference field satisfies $B_{p,\mathrm{ref}}^2=\frac{\mu_0^2I_p^2R_0}{2V}$. The reference field is an effective current-based scale rather than a pointwise poloidal field. The normalization requires nonzero $I_p$ and positive evaluation volume. It is neither an average of local pressure-to-field ratios nor an unnormalized pressure. Unlike [toroidal beta](name:toroidal_beta), it uses the current-based poloidal scale.

definition: Non-negative total power deposited on a single divertor target by recombination processes, summing the plasma-ion and neutral-particle recombination channels at the plasma-material interface, in W. It is inferred from edge plasma simulations or from particle flux measurements combined with surface energy-release models.
documentation:
This quantity captures the combined recombination power delivered to a single divertor target, encompassing two physically distinct contributions: energy released when plasma ions recombine at or near the target surface (the plasma channel, quantified by plasma_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination) and energy deposited when neutral particles undergo recombination into lower-energy bound states at the material wall (the neutral channel, quantified by [neutral_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination](name:neutral_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination)).

The total recombination power at the target decomposes additively:

$$
P_{\rm rec,target} = P_{\rm rec,plasma} + P_{\rm rec,neutral}
$$

where $P_{\rm rec,plasma}$ is the ion-recombination contribution and $P_{\rm rec,neutral}$ is the neutral-particle recombination contribution, both in W.

This target-localized quantity is a spatial specialization of [power_due_to_recombination](name:power_due_to_recombination), which describes power deposited on plasma-facing materials by recombination processes without restriction to a particular surface location. In attached divertor operation, recombination power at the target is a minor fraction of the total heat load; in detached or high-recycling regimes, surface and volumetric recombination become significant energy sinks that reduce the conducted and convected flux reaching the target. It is inferred from edge plasma simulations or from particle flux measurements combined with surface energy-release models, and is non-negative by definition.
name: power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination

definition: Reciprocal square of total magnetic-field strength, providing a positive magnetic-geometry factor for equilibrium and flux-surface-averaged transport relations.
documentation:
The inverse square of total magnetic-field strength is a local magnetic-geometry factor that increases as the total field weakens and remains positive wherever the field magnitude is nonzero.

It is defined as the reciprocal of the [square of magnetic-field magnitude](name:square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude):

$$
B^{-2} = \frac{1}{B^2} = \frac{1}{\lvert \mathbf{B} \rvert^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic-field vector and $B$ is its magnitude.

The quantity applies to the full magnetic field in an equilibrium plasma, including all vector components and without restriction to a particle population. At the parent level it is a local quantity with no flux-surface or volume aggregation; it is distinct from the squared field magnitude itself and from the reciprocal square of any selected field component.

The [flux-surface-averaged inverse square of magnetic-field magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude) is obtained by applying a flux-surface average to this local factor. The averaging is a separate aggregation operation and does not alter the reciprocal-square transformation.
name: inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude

definition: Signed magnetic flux through a surface bounded by the contour formed by intersecting the magnetic surface through the evaluation point with a plane of constant vertical coordinate Z. For a flat integration surface, the normal points upward, toward increasing Z. In axisymmetric cylindrical coordinates, the full flux is ψ(R,Z) = 2π ∫₀ᴿ B_Z(R′,Z) R′ dR′, in Wb, where B_Z is the vertical magnetic-field component. This is the full surface integral, not flux divided by 2π, a normalized coordinate, or a spatial average.
documentation: Poloidal magnetic flux, commonly denoted ψ or Φ_p, labels magnetic surfaces in axisymmetric equilibrium and can be represented on spatial grids or used as a radial profile coordinate. In axisymmetry, its integration surface is a horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis and bounded by the toroidal circle through the evaluation point; upward magnetic-field threading contributes positively. Unlike toroidal magnetic flux, it does not integrate the toroidal field through a poloidal cross-section. It includes plasma-generated and external contributions, rather than selecting only external flux. This record describes the general flux function, not its evaluation at a designated magnetic axis, plasma boundary, measurement position, or individual flux loop.

definition: Angular expansion coefficients specify how individual basis terms contribute to the cross-sectional shape of a magnetic flux surface. For the selected shape function f, angular parameterization θ, and angular basis functions b_k, the coefficients c_k satisfy f(θ) = Σ_k c_k b_k(θ), where k indexes expansion terms. Their values depend on these selections; no particular harmonic or trigonometric parity is imposed at this parent level. The coefficients describe the specified flux surface, not a surface average or an enclosed-volume integral. They are dimensionless, with unit 1.
documentation:
Flux-surface shape coefficients give the amplitudes of terms in an angular expansion describing cross-sectional geometry. The coefficient vector collects these amplitudes for the specified flux surface; its components label expansion terms rather than spatial directions.

For a chosen angular shape representation, the coefficients enter through:

$$
f(\theta) = \sum_k c_k b_k(\theta)
$$

where $f$ is the represented cross-sectional shape function, $\theta$ is its angular parameter, $k$ indexes the expansion terms, $c_k$ is the coefficient of term $k$, and $b_k$ is the corresponding angular basis function.

The coefficients describe the specified flux surface, not a surface average or an enclosed-volume integral. Their values depend on the selected shape function, angular parameterization, and basis; no particular harmonic or trigonometric parity is imposed at this parent level.

The [sine coefficient of a flux surface](name:sine_coefficient_of_flux_surface) specializes this definition to sine terms in the angular decomposition. An individual expansion coefficient is distinct from an overall geometric descriptor such as [triangularity](name:triangularity_of_flux_surface).

definition: Flux-surface-averaged magnetic-field magnitude is the mean strength of the total equilibrium field, with the local magnitude taken before averaging.
documentation:
Flux-surface-averaged magnetic-field magnitude is the mean strength of the total equilibrium [magnetic field](name:magnetic_field) on each closed nested magnetic flux surface.

Its defining relation is

$$
\langle B\rangle = \oint B\,dS/|\nabla\psi| \,/\, \oint dS/|\nabla\psi|
$$

where $B$ is the local total [magnetic-field magnitude](name:magnetic_field_magnitude), $\langle B\rangle$ is its flux-surface average, $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic-flux label, $\nabla\psi$ is the gradient of that label, and $dS$ is the area element of the closed surface over which both integrals are taken.

All equilibrium magnetic-field components contribute to the local magnitude before averaging. This quantity is not a selected field component, a pointwise field strength, or the magnitude of a surface-averaged field vector. It is positive for a nonvanishing equilibrium field.

The [flux-surface-averaged squared magnetic-field magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude) instead averages the square of the local field strength. That second moment is not the square of this mean unless the field strength is constant over the surface.

The flux-surface average is the average of a quantity over a closed magnetic flux surface, weighted by the inverse magnitude of the poloidal flux gradient.

The magnitude is the Euclidean norm of a vector quantity, or the modulus of a complex one.
