definition: Polarization angle of motional Stark effect emission at a constraint position: the angular orientation of the linear-polarization axis of the beam emission for the specified neutral-beam and viewing geometry, whether realized as an observed angle or as the angle consistent with a reconstructed equilibrium state.
documentation:
Polarization angle of motional Stark effect emission at a constraint position is the angular orientation of the linear-polarization axis of the light emitted by injected neutral-beam atoms, for the specified neutral-beam and viewing geometry.

The polarization angle is defined by

$$
\alpha = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left(\hat{\mathbf p}\cdot\hat{\mathbf e}_2,\;\hat{\mathbf p}\cdot\hat{\mathbf e}_1\right) \pmod{\pi}
$$

where $\alpha$ is the polarization angle, $\hat{\mathbf p}$ is a unit vector along the linear-polarization axis of the emission, and $\hat{\mathbf e}_1$ and $\hat{\mathbf e}_2$ are orthonormal unit vectors spanning the viewing plane perpendicular to the line of sight: $\hat{\mathbf e}_1$ sets the angular zero and $\hat{\mathbf e}_2$ sets the positive angular direction. Reduction modulo a half-turn reflects that linear polarization defines an axis rather than an oriented vector, so orientations differing by a half-turn are equivalent.

The quantity is specific to the constraint position and to the stated beam and viewing geometry; it is not an average over positions, beams, or sightlines. It may denote the observed emission polarization orientation or the orientation that a reconstructed equilibrium state implies for the same geometry; both realizations denote the same physical angle.

It is not a residual between observed and equilibrium-consistent values, not a statistical weight, and not the magnetic-field pitch angle: the correspondence between this angle and the local magnetic-field pitch depends on the beam velocity, the viewing geometry, and the selected Stark polarization component. It is a geometry-specific form of the polarization angle, and it differs from the [Faraday angle](name:faraday_angle), which is a propagation-induced rotation of polarization rather than an emission polarization orientation.

Sign convention: Positive when the polarization axis rotates from the zero-angle reference direction $\hat{\mathbf e}_1$ toward the positive reference direction $\hat{\mathbf e}_2$ within the viewing plane.
name: polarization_angle_at_constraint_position

definition: Toroidal magnetic flux at the selected plasma boundary is the net flux of toroidal magnetic field through the poloidal cross-section enclosed by the selected plasma boundary, including externally imposed and plasma-poloidal-current contributions. At each equilibrium time slice, it is the scalar integral Φ = ∫Ω Bφ(R,Z) dA_RZ, in Wb, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius, Z is vertical height, and φ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above +Z; positive flux is in the direction of increasing φ. The selected boundary is the magnetic flux surface used by fixed-boundary codes, typically chosen at psi_norm = 99.x% of the separatrix, and is not necessarily the last closed magnetic flux surface.
documentation: Toroidal magnetic flux at the selected plasma boundary is the net flux of the toroidal magnetic-field component through the poloidal cross-section enclosed by the selected plasma boundary. It is the boundary value of toroidal magnetic flux used to define toroidal-flux radial labels. Here the selected boundary is the magnetic flux surface used by fixed-boundary codes, typically chosen at psi_norm = 99.x% of the separatrix, rather than necessarily the last closed magnetic flux surface. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height, the boundary toroidal flux is defined by $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor},b} = \int_{\Omega_b} \mathbf{B}\cdot\hat{\phi}\, dA_{RZ} = \int_{\Omega_b} B_\phi(R,Z)\, dA_{RZ} = \int_{\Omega_b} F(\psi(R,Z))/R\, dA_{RZ}$, where $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor},b}$ is this boundary toroidal flux, $\Omega_b$ is the selected-boundary-enclosed region in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field, $B_\phi$ is its toroidal component in tesla, $dA_{RZ}$ is the poloidal cross-sectional area element in square meters, $F(\psi)=R B_\phi$ is the poloidal-current function in tesla meters, and $\psi$ is the equilibrium poloidal magnetic-flux label. The geometric measure of $\Omega_b$ is the poloidal cross-sectional area enclosed by the selected boundary. $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor},b}$ includes both externally imposed toroidal-field flux and the contribution associated with plasma poloidal current, and is distinct from [toroidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary due to poloidal current](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary_due_to_poloidal_current), which contains only that plasma-current contribution. It also differs from [poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary), which is magnetic flux through a horizontal disk rather than through the boundary-enclosed poloidal cross-section. Sign convention: Positive when the net toroidal magnetic field threading the selected-plasma-boundary poloidal cross-section points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$. The quantity is evaluated at each equilibrium time slice.
enclosing_statements: Description of the plasma boundary used by fixed-boundary codes and typically chosen at psi_norm = 99.x% of the separatrix
Set of equilibria at various time slices

definition: Alpha angle specifying the first inclination of an oblique poloidal-field-coil conductor-element cross-section, measured from the outward major-radius direction.
documentation:
Alpha angle $\alpha$ specifies the inclination of the first cross-sectional axis at a coil conductor element. It applies to the oblique trapezoidal or parallelogram cross-sectional geometry of an active poloidal-field coil.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the angle is defined by

$$
\alpha = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left(\mathbf{a}_1\cdot\hat{Z},\,\mathbf{a}_1\cdot\hat{R}\right)
$$

where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The vector $\mathbf{a}_1$ points along the first cross-sectional axis; $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{Z}$ are the outward major-radius and upward unit vectors, respectively. The function $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the quadrant-resolved angle from the radial and vertical projections.

This is an individual-element shape parameter, not an average over the coil. The [tilt angle of the coil conductor element](name:tilt_angle_of_coil_conductor_element) specifies the separate second inclination of the same cross-section.

Sign convention: Positive when the first cross-sectional axis rotates from the outward major-radius direction toward increasing vertical height.

definition: Lower photon-energy boundary of an X-ray detection or emission energy band, expressed in eV. For photon counting, it is the threshold assigned to the specified detector pixel or channel: an incident photon is eligible for counting only if its energy exceeds this value. documentation: This quantity specifies the low-energy edge of a spectral window, paired with upper_photon_energy at the high-energy edge. For emission profiles, the quantity instead delimits the included emission band without imposing a detector-counting interpretation.

definition: Elongation of a flux surface is the ratio of its poloidal cross-section’s vertical extent to its radial extent, independent of overall size. In the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius, φ is toroidal angle, and Z is vertical height, it is κ = (Z_max − Z_min)/(R_max − R_min), using the vertical and major-radius extrema of the cross-section. It applies to an individual surface of constant poloidal magnetic flux ψ(R, Z) in a nested-flux-surface configuration, not an average over nested surfaces. The cross-section need not be elliptical; for an ellipse, the ratio equals the vertical to horizontal semi-axis ratio. It is not restricted to the plasma boundary. The quantity is dimensionless, with unit 1.
documentation:
Elongation of flux surface

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the defining relation is:

$$
\kappa = (Z_{\max} - Z_{\min})/(R_{\max} - R_{\min})
$$

where $\kappa$ is the elongation, $Z_{\max}$ and $Z_{\min}$ are the maximum and minimum vertical coordinates of the cross-section, and $R_{\max}$ and $R_{\min}$ are its maximum and minimum major radii.

The quantity applies to an individual flux surface, not an average over nested surfaces. For an elliptical cross-section, it equals the ratio of the vertical to horizontal semi-axes; the extent-based definition does not require an ellipse. It is not restricted to the plasma boundary: evaluating it there gives the [elongation of the plasma boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary).

The [derivative of elongation with respect to normalized minor radius](name:derivative_of_elongation_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_normalized_minor_radius) describes how this ratio changes between neighboring surfaces, rather than the shape ratio itself.

A surface formed by points sharing the same magnetic-flux label in a nested-flux-surface configuration. Where $\psi(R, Z) = \mathrm{const}$, $\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux.

definition: Angular expansion coefficients specify how individual basis terms contribute to the cross-sectional shape of a magnetic flux surface.
documentation:
Flux-surface shape coefficients give the amplitudes of terms in an angular expansion describing cross-sectional geometry. The coefficient vector collects these amplitudes for the specified flux surface; its components label expansion terms rather than spatial directions.

For a chosen angular shape representation, the coefficients enter through:

$$
f(\theta) = \sum_k c_k b_k(\theta)
$$

where $f$ is the represented cross-sectional shape function, $\theta$ is its angular parameter, $k$ indexes the expansion terms, $c_k$ is the coefficient of term $k$, and $b_k$ is the corresponding angular basis function.

The coefficients describe the specified flux surface, not a surface average or an enclosed-volume integral. Their values depend on the selected shape function, angular parameterization, and basis; no particular harmonic or trigonometric parity is imposed at this parent level.

The [sine coefficient of a flux surface](name:sine_coefficient_of_flux_surface) specializes this definition to sine terms in the angular decomposition. An individual expansion coefficient is distinct from an overall geometric descriptor such as [triangularity](name:triangularity_of_flux_surface).

definition: Instantaneous injection rate of ethylene (C2H4) gas into the plasma vessel, expressed as equivalent electrons per second with each molecule counted as 16 equivalent electrons.
documentation:
Ethylene (C2H4) is a two-carbon, four-hydrogen molecule used as a gaseous source of both carbon and hydrogen in plasma fueling and wall-conditioning experiments. The source rate is the instantaneous equivalent-electron delivery rate to the plasma vessel, where each molecule is assigned 16 equivalent electrons based on the total atomic electron inventory of the molecular formula.

The equivalent-electron rate $\dot{N}_\mathrm{eq}$ relates to the molecular injection rate $\dot{N}_\mathrm{C_2H_4}$ by

$$
\dot{N}_\mathrm{eq} = 16\,\dot{N}_\mathrm{C_2H_4}
$$

where the factor $16 = 2Z_\mathrm{C} + 4Z_\mathrm{H}$, with $Z_\mathrm{C} = 6$ the carbon atomic number and $Z_\mathrm{H} = 1$ the hydrogen atomic number.

The injection rate is inferred from valve conductance calibrations and upstream pressure measurements. Its time-integral gives the [accumulated ethylene count](name:accumulated_ethylene_count), which tracks the total equivalent-electron inventory delivered since plasma breakdown. Related molecular and atomic injection rates include [silane_source_rate](name:silane_source_rate) for SiH4 and [hydrogen_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection](name:hydrogen_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection) for atomic hydrogen delivery.

Sign convention: Positive when ethylene gas flows from the injection system into the plasma vessel.
name: ethylene_equivalent_electron_source_rate

definition: Major-radius coordinate of a magnetic flux surface at its inboard midplane intersection, locating the high-field-side point relative to the toroidal symmetry axis. It is the minimum major radius on that surface, R_in(S) = min_{x in S} R(x), with R_in(S) < R_axis, where R_axis is the major radius of the magnetic axis. The coordinate is the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, expressed in m. At each equilibrium time slice, these scalar values form a one-dimensional radial profile as a function of poloidal flux.
documentation:
This quantity is the major-radius coordinate of the point where a magnetic flux surface intersects the inboard midplane, identifying the high-field-side location of that surface relative to the toroidal symmetry axis. It is a locus-specific form of the [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate).

For a magnetic flux surface $\mathcal{S}$, the inboard-midplane radial coordinate is defined by

$$
R_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S}) = R\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S})\right)
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S})$ is the quantity defined here, $R(\mathbf{x})$ is the major-radius coordinate of spatial position $\mathbf{x}$, $\mathcal{S}$ is the specified magnetic flux surface, and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S})$ is its inboard midplane intersection. The coordinates are expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The scope is one coordinate value for each specified magnetic flux surface at its inboard, high-field-side midplane intersection. It is not a flux-surface average, a poloidal or toroidal average, or the corresponding outboard-midplane coordinate; the latter is represented by [radial coordinate at outboard midplane](name:radial_coordinate_at_outboard_midplane). Unlike [radial magnetic field](name:radial_magnetic_field), this quantity describes the location of a surface and not a magnetic-field component.

definition: Volume enclosed by a magnetic flux surface, accumulated over its full interior rather than only the shell between adjacent surfaces.
documentation:
Volume of flux surface

The volume is defined by

$$
V = \int_{\Omega} d^3\mathbf{x}
$$

where $V$ is the enclosed volume, $\Omega$ is the spatial domain inside the selected magnetic flux surface, $\mathbf{x}$ is spatial position, and $d^3\mathbf{x}$ is the differential volume element.

The integral covers the entire enclosed region and excludes space outside the selected surface. It is not a local shell volume; differences between enclosed volumes give the volume between neighboring surfaces. For successively enclosing nested surfaces, the volume increases from zero at the magnetic axis.

When the selected surface coincides with the plasma boundary, this quantity equals the [volume enclosed by the plasma boundary](name:volume_of_plasma_boundary). The [poloidal-flux derivative](name:derivative_of_volume_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate) and [toroidal-flux derivative](name:derivative_of_volume_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate) describe its rate of change with their respective flux coordinates and provide the geometric measures relating flux-coordinate intervals to enclosed shell volumes.

definition: Ratio of the squared gradient magnitude of the length-valued toroidal-flux coordinate to squared major radius, defining a local equilibrium metric coefficient. It is calculated pointwise as G = |∇ρ_tor|²/R², without spatial averaging, using the Euclidean norm and the spatial gradient operator. The length-valued coordinate ρ_tor retains its prescribed scale, with no boundary normalization or substitution of an arbitrary flux label. In the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, R is the distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, φ is the toroidal angle, and Z is the vertical height. The denominator is R², not its inverse. The unit is m^-2.
documentation:
Ratio of the squared toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient magnitude to squared major radius is a local equilibrium metric coefficient. It encodes flux-surface spacing with inverse-square major-radius weighting.

The defining relation is:

$$
G = \frac{|\nabla \rho_{\mathrm{tor}}|^2}{R^2}
$$

where $G$ is this local coefficient, $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the length-valued toroidal-flux coordinate, and $\nabla$ is the spatial gradient operator. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is the distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the vertical height.

The toroidal-flux coordinate retains its prescribed scale; no boundary normalization or substitution of an arbitrary flux label is implied. The denominator is squared major radius, not its inverse. The squared gradient magnitude distinguishes this coefficient from inverse squared major radius alone.

This quantity is a pointwise ratio without spatial averaging. Its flux-surface-averaged counterpart averages the complete ratio over a closed magnetic flux surface; it is not the ratio of separately averaged numerator and denominator.

$$a/b$$

The magnitude is the Euclidean norm of a vector quantity, or the modulus of a complex one.

The ratio is one quantity divided by another.

The square is a scalar quantity multiplied by itself, or a vector's dot product with itself.
name: ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_major_radius

definition: Reciprocal square of total magnetic-field strength, providing a positive magnetic-geometry factor for equilibrium and flux-surface-averaged transport relations. It is evaluated locally as 1/|B|^2 for the full equilibrium magnetic-field vector, including all vector components and without restriction to a particle population, with no flux-surface or volume aggregation; its unit is T^-2.
documentation:
The inverse square of total magnetic-field strength is a local magnetic-geometry factor that increases as the total field weakens and remains positive wherever the field magnitude is nonzero.

It is defined as the reciprocal of the [square of magnetic-field magnitude](name:square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude):

$$
B^{-2} = \frac{1}{B^2} = \frac{1}{\lvert \mathbf{B} \rvert^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic-field vector and $B$ is its magnitude.

The quantity applies to the full magnetic field in an equilibrium plasma, including all vector components and without restriction to a particle population. At the parent level it is a local quantity with no flux-surface or volume aggregation; it is distinct from the squared field magnitude itself and from the reciprocal square of any selected field component.

The [flux-surface-averaged inverse square of magnetic-field magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude) is obtained by applying a flux-surface average to this local factor. The averaging is a separate aggregation operation and does not alter the reciprocal-square transformation.
name: inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude

definition: Dimensionless scalar factor assigned to the residual between modeled and reference line-integrated electron density for a single interferometer beam, controlling that residual's relative contribution to a weighted objective. For a quadratic objective, the beam contribution is Phi_b = w_b r_b^2, where w_b is this weight and r_b is the beam residual. The weight is assigned per beam; no averaging or normalization across beams is implied. Unit: 1.
documentation: This quantity weights one interferometer beam's line-integrated electron-density constraint, rather than an entire interferometer system or another constraint type. It is neither the electron density nor its residual or uncertainty. It is the general parent of equilibrium_weight_of_interferometer_beam, which restricts the same weighting role to an equilibrium objective. No particular procedure for selecting the weight or normalizing the residual is specified.
name: weight_of_interferometer_beam

definition: Cross-sectional area of a plasma current filament element, expressed in m^2. The cross-section's orientation and the method of obtaining its area are not specified.
documentation: This scalar describes the area of a filament element's cross-section, rather than its height, width or inclined-side length. Unlike poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_plasma_filament, it does not specify that the cross-section lies in the poloidal plane. No particular cross-sectional shape or calculation from the filament dimensions is prescribed.

definition: Absolute thermodynamic temperature of a selected sensor, represented by the local temperature at its thermocouple junction and obtained by thermocouple measurement, in K. It applies to one sensor member, not to an average or other aggregation over the sensor set.
documentation: This scalar quantity describes the local thermal state at the thermocouple junction of an individual sensor associated with a structural component. The enclosing set of sensors provides collection context only; the value is not a sum or average over that set. Its sensor locus distinguishes it from coolant temperatures at inlet, outlet, or plant-component ports and from temperatures assigned to specifically named hardware such as a neutron detector or coil conductor. It describes thermal state rather than the acceleration, displacement, or strain measured by other structural instrumentation.

definition: Vertical coordinate of a plasma filament geometry point, giving its signed height from the zero-height plane in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
Vertical coordinate of a plasma filament geometry point specifies its signed height in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the vertical coordinate parallel to the toroidal symmetry axis.

The coordinate is defined by:

$$
Z = \mathbf{x}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}}
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is the position vector of the specified point relative to the coordinate origin and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the unit vector along the positive symmetry-axis direction.

The specified point is the reference point for an oblique cross-section or the second endpoint of the central segment for a thick-line cross-section. The quantity applies to one filament geometry point, not an average over filaments or a coordinate of the plasma boundary. Unlike the [vertical outline of a plasma filament](name:vertical_outline_of_plasma_filament), it specifies a point location rather than a contour.

Sign convention: Positive when the specified point lies on the positive-$Z$ side of the zero-height plane.

Each element holds a cross-sectional area and time-resolved current, enabling the plasma to be modelled as a distributed current source for electromagnetic circuit and equilibrium calculations.

definition: Cumulative equivalent-electron inventory of all gas species delivered by injection after plasma breakdown, summed across species.
documentation:
This quantity is the cumulative equivalent-electron inventory of gas introduced into the plasma by injection after plasma breakdown. It combines all injected gas species into one total inventory.

The total is defined by

$$
N_{\mathrm{eq}}(t) = \sum_s z_s N_s(t)
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{eq}}(t)$ is the accumulated equivalent-electron count, $s$ identifies an injected gas species, $N_s(t)$ is the cumulative number of particles of species $s$ delivered since plasma breakdown, and $z_s$ is the equivalent-electron contribution per particle; for an atomic species, $z_s$ is its atomic number, while for a molecule it is the sum of the atomic numbers of its constituent atoms.

The quantity applies to all gas species and uses a cumulative sum over the post-breakdown injection history. It excludes gas introduced during prefill before plasma breakdown, instantaneous injection rates, and any single-species inventory such as [accumulated hydrogen count due to gas injection](name:accumulated_hydrogen_count_due_to_gas_injection).

It is the post-breakdown counterpart of the prefill inventory [accumulated total prefill gas count](name:accumulated_total_prefill_gas_count); the two quantities differ by the injection phase they accumulate.
name: accumulated_total_gas_count

definition: Full thickness of a rectangular plasma filament cross-section, measured along the in-plane direction normal to the filament's central segment. It is the transverse side length of the rectangle, complementing the tangential length measured along the segment. The central segment lies in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The thickness is a non-negative geometric length expressed in m.
documentation:
Thickness of a plasma filament is the full transverse extent of a rectangular (thick-line) filament cross-section, measured in the local plane of the element along the direction normal to the filament's central segment. The central segment lies in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and the local tangential-normal basis is defined within that plane: the tangential direction follows the central segment while the normal direction is the in-plane perpendicular. It is a full side length, not a half-width.

For a rectangular filament cross-section, the cross-sectional area is the product of the two full local side lengths:

$$
A_\mathrm{fil} = L_\mathrm{tan}\, t
$$

where $A_\mathrm{fil}$ is the filament cross-sectional area in $\mathrm{m}^2$, $L_\mathrm{tan}$ is the tangential length in $\mathrm{m}$, and $t$ is the thickness in $\mathrm{m}$. When the local tangential and normal directions align with the cylindrical axes, the thickness coincides with either the width (radial $R$-direction extent) or the [height](name:height_of_plasma_filament) (vertical $Z$-direction extent) of the same rectangular cross-section.

In equilibrium filament descriptions, the thickness is set by the chosen local geometric representation of a discrete current-carrying plasma element. For a thick-line element it is specified directly as the rectangle side perpendicular to the central segment.

The value is a non-negative geometric length governed by the spatial resolution and local size of the filament representation. No universal device-independent numerical range applies; it should be interpreted relative to the associated tangential length and to neighboring filament spacing.
enclosing_statements: The element is approximated by a rectangle defined by a central segment and a thickness in the direction perpendicular to the segment
Cross-sectional shape of the element

Set of plasma elements Array of discrete plasma current-carrying filamentary elements representing the axisymmetric plasma current distribution. Each element holds a cross-sectional area and time-resolved current, enabling the plasma to be modelled as a distributed current source for electromagnetic circuit and equilibrium calculations.
name: thickness_of_plasma_filament
source_descriptions: Thickness

definition: Non-negative curvature radius of one arc-of-circle segment used to approximate the cross-sectional contour of a poloidal field coil. The contour lies in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height.
documentation:
Radius of a poloidal-field-coil arc is the non-negative circle radius of a single circular segment of the coil cross-sectional contour, taken in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. The conductor or winding-pack boundary is approximated by connected circular arcs, and this quantity sets the local radius of curvature of one such arc.

For a circular contour segment, the curvature radius $\rho$ (in m) is the inverse magnitude of the planar curvature $\kappa$ (in m$^{-1}$) of the boundary curve in the $(R, Z)$ cross-section:

$$
\rho = \frac{1}{|\kappa|}
$$

where a finite physical arc has $\rho > 0$, and as $\rho$ grows the segment approaches a straight line ($\kappa \to 0$). Each arc is anchored by a start point in the poloidal plane: its major-radius coordinate is given by major_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil and its vertical coordinate by [height_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil); both together with $\rho$ are needed to locate and shape one arc, with the end of each arc coinciding with the start of the next.

The value is determined from the designed circular-arc contour, from CAD geometry, or by fitting circular arcs to surveyed boundary points. Small radii represent tightly rounded corners and compact winding-pack features, while larger radii represent gently curved coil sides; the magnitude scales with coil aperture, winding-pack dimensions, and mechanical-clearance requirements. An analogous arc-of-circle convention applies to iron core segment boundaries via radius_of_iron_core_segment.
name: radius_of_poloidal_field_coil

definition: Dimensionless collisionality for a specified pair of particle species, obtained by dividing their collision frequency by the characteristic transit frequency: nu_ab_star = nu_ab / nu_transit. Both frequencies have reciprocal-time units, and the resulting quantity has unit 1.
documentation: This quantity describes the strength of collisional relaxation between two specified particle species relative to transit motion in the local gyrokinetic model. Its species-pair indices identify the interacting populations. Unlike the collision frequency itself, it is dimensionless. It is not restricted to electrons or to the pedestal top, and its characteristic-transit-frequency normalization differs from the trapped-electron bounce-frequency normalization used by the neighbouring electron-collisionality records.

documentation: This scalar describes the line or groove density of a diffraction grating used in charge-exchange or ultraviolet spectroscopy. Both source descriptions identify the same quantity, using “lines” and “grooves” synonymously. It characterizes the grating rather than its surface curvature, a detector pixel's assigned wavelength, or a spectrometer channel's spectral width or instrument function.

definition: Weight of an interferometer beam is the scalar factor assigned to the residual for one interferometer beam, controlling how strongly that beam's line-integrated electron-density constraint contributes to a weighted objective. It applies per beam, not to an entire interferometer system.
documentation:
Weight of an interferometer beam is the scalar factor assigned to the residual for one interferometer beam in a weighted objective. The residual is associated with that beam's line-integrated electron-density constraint, so the weight controls that beam's relative influence among simultaneously weighted constraints.

For a quadratic weighted objective, the contribution from one beam is represented by:

$$
\Phi_b = w_b r_b^2
$$

where $w_b$ is the weight of the interferometer beam, $r_b$ is the residual between the modeled and reference line-integrated electron density for the same beam, and $\Phi_b$ is that beam's contribution to the objective.

The scope is a single interferometer beam. No summation, averaging, or normalization over multiple beams is implied; a set of beams has separate weights and separate residual contributions. This quantity is not the line-integrated electron density, not the residual itself, not an uncertainty, and not a weight for a whole interferometer system or for other constraint types.

The [equilibrium weight of an interferometer beam](name:equilibrium_weight_of_interferometer_beam) is the equilibrium-specific specialization of this parent quantity. Changing $w_b$ changes only the relative contribution of the corresponding beam term in the objective; it does not change the definition of the beam residual.
name: weight_of_interferometer_beam

definition: Non-negative geometric separation between the inner and outer material interfaces of a breeder blanket layer along the specified thickness direction.
documentation:
Non-negative geometric separation between the inner and outer material interfaces of a breeder blanket layer is the local through-thickness of that layer along the specified thickness direction. The quantity applies to a single material or functional layer within the blanket, not to the total breeder blanket module build.

The layer thickness is defined by the separation of the two bounding interfaces along the thickness coordinate:

$$
d_\ell = \left|s_{\ell,\mathrm{out}} - s_{\ell,\mathrm{in}}\right|
$$

where $d_\ell$ is the layer thickness in m, and $s_{\ell,\mathrm{in}}$ and $s_{\ell,\mathrm{out}}$ are the signed coordinates in m of the inner and outer layer interfaces along the specified thickness direction.

It is not the toroidal width, poloidal height, surface extent, or volume-equivalent thickness of the layer. It is distinct from module-level quantities such as thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module, [lower_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:lower_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module), and [upper_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:upper_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module). For a radially stacked layer, the thickness direction is the cylindrical $\hat{R}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.
enclosing_statements: Set of layers in the blanket module
Set of modules composing the blanket
name: thickness_of_breeder_blanket_layer
source_descriptions: Thickness of this layer evaluated at the midplane

definition: Shift of pellet-material deposition relative to its ablation location caused by E×B drift, expressed as a difference in normalized toroidal flux coordinate.
documentation:
The pellet deposition displacement describes the shift of ablated pellet material from its ablation location to its final deposition location attributable to E-cross-B drift. It is expressed as a difference in normalized toroidal flux coordinate.

The displacement is defined by deposition minus ablation:

$$
\Delta\rho_{\mathrm{tor},\mathrm{N}} = \rho_{\mathrm{tor},\mathrm{N},\mathrm{dep}} - \rho_{\mathrm{tor},\mathrm{N},\mathrm{abl}}
$$

where $\Delta\rho_{\mathrm{tor},\mathrm{N}}$ is the pellet deposition displacement, and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor},\mathrm{N},\mathrm{dep}}$ and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor},\mathrm{N},\mathrm{abl}}$ are the normalized toroidal flux coordinates at the final deposition and ablation locations, respectively.

Each value concerns material ablated at the corresponding location along the pellet path, not a path-integrated displacement. Only the shift attributed to E-cross-B drift is included. This coordinate difference is neither an absolute deposition coordinate nor a geometric distance or drift velocity; it describes redistribution of ablated material rather than the injection motion characterized by the [initial pellet velocity](name:initial_velocity_of_pellet).
enclosing_statements: 1-D profiles of plasma and pellet along the pellet path
Set of pellets ablated in the plasma at a given time
Description of the pellets launched at various time slices. The time of this structure corresponds to the full ablation of the pellet inside the plasma.

definition: Outer radius of a plasma filament is the geometric radius of the outer circular boundary of the annular cross-section representing a current-carrying plasma filament. It marks the external boundary of the conducting annular region. In the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, it is the nonnegative distance r_outer = sqrt((R - R_c)^2 + (Z - Z_c)^2) from the cross-section center (R_c, Z_c) to any point (R, Z) on the outer circular boundary, where R is major radius, φ is toroidal angle and Z is vertical height. It is a single geometric radius for that boundary, not an average over the conducting region, and is expressed in metres (m).
documentation:
Outer radius of a plasma filament is the geometric radius of the outer circular boundary of the annular cross-section representing a current-carrying plasma filament. It marks the external boundary of the conducting annular region; material outside this boundary is not part of that annular filament cross-section.

For the outer circular boundary in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the outer radius $r_\mathrm{outer}$ is the distance from the filament cross-section center $(R_c, Z_c)$ to any point $(R, Z)$ on that boundary:

$$
r_\mathrm{outer} = \sqrt{(R - R_c)^2 + (Z - Z_c)^2}
$$

where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical height, $(R_c, Z_c)$ is the center of the annular cross-section, and $(R, Z)$ lies on the outer circular boundary.

The quantity applies only to the outer boundary of an annular plasma-filament cross-section and is a single geometric radius for that boundary, not an average over the conducting region. It is the outer member of radius of a plasma filament, paired with the [inner radius](name:inner_radius_of_plasma_filament) $r_\mathrm{inner}$; by definition $0 \le r_\mathrm{inner} \le r_\mathrm{outer}$, and the current-carrying cross-section occupies the annular region between the two radii. For the same annular geometry, the area of a plasma filament $A$ satisfies $A = \pi(r_\mathrm{outer}^2 - r_\mathrm{inner}^2)$, where $A$ is the area of the annular plasma-filament cross-section and $\pi$ is the circle constant. This quantity excludes the major radius of the filament center about the toroidal symmetry axis and rectangular cross-section dimensions such as [plasma filament width](name:plasma_filament_width) and [height of a plasma filament](name:height_of_plasma_filament).
name: outer_radius_of_plasma_filament

definition: Toroidal reference magnetic field is the signed toroidal component of the equilibrium magnetic field at the reference point whose major radius is the reference major radius, expressed in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
Toroidal reference magnetic field is the signed toroidal component of the equilibrium magnetic field at a specified reference point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The reference point has major radius equal to the [reference major radius](name:reference_major_radius).

The defining projection is:

$$
B_{\phi,\mathrm{ref}} = \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{eq}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ref}}) \cdot \hat{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ref}})
$$

where $B_{\phi,\mathrm{ref}}$ is the toroidal reference magnetic field, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is the equilibrium magnetic field, $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ref}}=(R_{\mathrm{ref}},\phi_{\mathrm{ref}},Z_{\mathrm{ref}})$ is the full reference point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the reference major radius, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing $\phi$. For an axisymmetric equilibrium, the value is independent of $\phi_{\mathrm{ref}}$.

This quantity is the reference-location specialization of [toroidal magnetic field](name:toroidal_magnetic_field). It is distinct from [toroidal magnetic field at magnetic axis](name:toroidal_magnetic_field_at_magnetic_axis), from the magnetic-field magnitude, and from [toroidal vacuum magnetic field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field).

Sign convention: Positive when $B_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
enclosing_statements: Physical quantities used for normalization (useful to link to the original simulation/experience)
name: toroidal_reference_magnetic_field
source_descriptions: Toroidal magnetic field at major radius r

definition: Poloidal magnetic flux is the signed magnetic flux through a horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis, labeling magnetic surfaces in axisymmetric equilibrium.
documentation:
Poloidal magnetic flux is the net magnetic flux through a horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis and bounded by the toroidal circle through the evaluation point. It specializes [magnetic flux](name:magnetic_flux) by specifying the integration surface and its orientation. In axisymmetric equilibrium, its level sets define magnetic surfaces.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counterclockwise when viewed from above, and $Z$ is vertical height. The full poloidal magnetic flux is defined by

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{p}}(R,Z) \equiv \psi(R,Z) = 2\pi \int_0^R B_Z(R',Z)\,R'\,dR'
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{p}}$, also denoted $\psi$, is the poloidal magnetic flux, $B_Z$ is the vertical magnetic-field component, and $R'$ is the radial integration variable. The factor $2\pi$ accounts for integration around the complete toroidal circle.

This quantity includes contributions from plasma currents and external sources, unlike [external magnetic flux](name:external_magnetic_flux), which excludes the plasma-generated contribution. It is the full flux, not flux divided by $2\pi$, a normalized coordinate, or a cross-sectional average. It differs from [toroidal magnetic flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux), which integrates the toroidal magnetic field through a poloidal cross-section.

The [magnetic-axis value](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis) and [plasma-boundary value](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary) are evaluations of this same function and provide the endpoint references for poloidal-flux normalization. For nested surfaces enclosing positive toroidal plasma current flowing toward increasing $\phi$, the poloidal flux decreases from the magnetic axis to the plasma boundary.

Sign convention: Positive when the magnetic field threading the horizontal disk has a net component toward increasing $Z$, along the upward surface normal.

definition: Real part of the first-order radial magnetic-vector-potential eigenfunction for a single toroidal mode in the vacuum region.
documentation:
The quantity is the real radial projection of the first-order perturbed magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction in the vacuum region for one toroidal Fourier mode. The real part is defined relative to the phase reference of that complex eigenfunction.

$$
A_{R,\mathrm{vac}}^{\mathrm{Re}} = \operatorname{Re}\!\left(\widetilde{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathrm{vac}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}}\right)
$$

Here $A_{R,\mathrm{vac}}^{\mathrm{Re}}$ is the requested real radial component, $\widetilde{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the complex first-order perturbed magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction in the vacuum region, $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the radial unit vector, and $\operatorname{Re}$ denotes the real-part operation. The radial direction is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies outside the plasma and to one toroidal Fourier mode; it is not summed over modes. It excludes the plasma-region perturbation, the imaginary component, and the unreduced complex radial component. The [radial perturbed vacuum magnetic vector potential](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential) is the full complex parent quantity, of which this entry is the real-part component. It is distinct from the [radial perturbed vacuum magnetic field](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field), which is a magnetic-field perturbation rather than a vector potential.

Sign convention: Positive when the real radial projection points toward increasing major radius $R$.

definition: Back-surface neutron energy flux is the local rate of neutron kinetic-energy transfer outward through an object's designated rear surface, per unit actual surface area and time. It is a scalar energy flux, not a neutron count flux, integrated power, or spatial maximum. Its unit is W.m^-2.
documentation:
Back-surface neutron energy flux is the local rate at which neutron kinetic energy crosses outward through an object's designated rear surface, per unit actual surface area and time. It is a scalar measure of energy transfer, not a neutron count rate.

The local energy flux is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{n,\mathrm{back}}^{E}(\mathbf r,t) = \frac{\partial^2 E_{n,\mathrm{out}}}{\partial A\,\partial t}(\mathbf r,t)
$$

where $\Gamma_{n,\mathrm{back}}^{E}$ is the back-surface neutron energy flux, $n$ identifies the neutron contributions, $\mathbf r$ is position on the back surface, $t$ is time, $E_{n,\mathrm{out}}$ is the cumulative kinetic energy carried by neutrons crossing outward through the surface, and $A$ is actual surface area.

The quantity applies locally over the object's designated back surface and aggregates the kinetic-energy contributions of outward-crossing neutrons across their energies. It excludes neutron number flux, neutron production within a volume, energy deposited inside material, power integrated over a surface, and a spatial maximum or average over the surface.

Integrating the local flux over a portion of the back surface gives the neutron power crossing outward through that portion. The [maximum of back-surface neutron flux](name:maximum_of_back_surface_neutron_flux) is the greatest local value over the applicable back surface; that maximum is not part of this local quantity.
name: back_surface_neutron_energy_flux

definition: Orientation indicator equal to the sign of the toroidal magnetic-field component on a flux surface in local gyrokinetic geometry.
documentation:
The toroidal magnetic-field sign specifies whether the equilibrium toroidal field component on a flux surface is directed along or opposite increasing toroidal angle in local gyrokinetic geometry.

For a nonzero toroidal magnetic-field component, the orientation indicator is defined by

$$
s_\phi = \operatorname{sgn}(B_\phi) = \frac{B_\phi}{|B_\phi|}
$$

where $s_\phi$ is the orientation indicator, $B_\phi$ is the toroidal magnetic-field component, and $\operatorname{sgn}$ is the sign function. The component is $B_\phi = \mathbf{B}\cdot\hat{\phi}$, where $\mathbf{B}$ is the equilibrium magnetic field and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector toward increasing toroidal angle. The right-handed cylindrical frame is $(R,\phi,Z)$, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

As the toroidal member of [parity](name:parity), this quantity retains only field orientation and takes the values $+1$ or $-1$; the two-valued indicator is undefined when the toroidal component vanishes. It does not specify field strength, plasma-current direction, or the even or odd symmetry of a gyrokinetic perturbation.

Sign convention: Positive when the toroidal magnetic-field component points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.
enclosing_statements: Flux surface characteristics
name: toroidal_parity
source_descriptions: Sign of the toroidal magnetic field

definition: Radial flux-surface location of the selected plasma boundary, expressed by the normalized poloidal flux coordinate. It is the linear normalized poloidal flux value, increasing from zero at the magnetic axis to one at the separatrix, of the closed flux surface taken as the plasma boundary; fixed-boundary equilibrium calculations commonly set it slightly below one to select a surface just inside the separatrix.
documentation:
The normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the plasma boundary is the value of the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate) on the closed flux surface selected as the plasma boundary. It is the linear normalized poloidal flux, labeling the boundary's radial position between the magnetic axis and the last closed flux surface.

Its value is the poloidal flux difference from the magnetic axis normalized to the axis-to-separatrix flux difference:

$$
\psi_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{boundary}} = \frac{\psi_{\mathrm{boundary}} - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}{\psi_{\mathrm{sep}} - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}
$$

where $\psi_{\mathrm{boundary}}$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) on the selected plasma-boundary surface, $\psi_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis), and $\psi_{\mathrm{sep}}$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at the separatrix (last closed flux surface).

The label equals zero at the magnetic axis and equals one when the selected plasma boundary coincides with the separatrix; a value below one selects an internal closed flux surface. Its defining role is to specify, for fixed-boundary equilibrium representations, which closed flux surface is taken as the plasma boundary, commonly a surface just inside the separatrix so that the boundary remains strictly closed.

This is the linear normalized poloidal flux value itself, not its square root, and it is a flux-surface label rather than a signed poloidal-flux value or a geometric minor-radius measure. It is distinct from the toroidal-flux-based boundary label normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the plasma boundary, and it belongs to the same locus-valued family as the normalized poloidal flux coordinate at minimum safety factor and the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the pedestal](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_pedestal).
enclosing_statements: Description of the plasma boundary used by fixed-boundary codes and typically chosen at psi_norm = 99.x% of the separatrix

definition: Squared toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient measuring local magnetic-flux-surface spacing through the associated contravariant metric coefficient.
documentation:
Squared toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient is a local equilibrium geometry coefficient describing the spatial variation of a toroidal magnetic-flux surface label. It is nonnegative and contains no directional projection, flux-surface averaging, or scaling by magnetic-field strength or major radius.

Its identification with the contravariant metric coefficient is

$$
g^{\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}} = |\nabla\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}|^2
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal magnetic-flux surface label, $\nabla$ denotes the spatial gradient with respect to physical position, and $g^{\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}}$ is the contravariant metric coefficient associated with that label. The [toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient magnitude](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude) is the unsquared parent quantity.

Flux-surface averaging gives the [flux-surface-averaged squared gradient magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude), rather than the square of the averaged gradient magnitude. Dividing the local coefficient by squared magnetic-field strength or squared major radius instead produces the corresponding geometry ratios; these scalings are not part of the unscaled coefficient.

The coordinate's scale is essential to the definition. Interpreting $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ as a dimensionless normalized flux radius makes this physical-space coefficient have inverse-square-length dimension, which is inconsistent with the declared dimensionless designation.

The magnitude is the Euclidean norm of a vector quantity, or the modulus of a complex one.

The square is a scalar quantity multiplied by itself, or a vector's dot product with itself.
name: square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude

definition: Dimensionless shape parameter for the plasma-boundary poloidal cross-section, expressing the aggregate inward radial displacement of its upper and lower extrema relative to the geometric center.
documentation:
Plasma-boundary triangularity is a dimensionless shaping parameter describing the asymmetry of the boundary’s poloidal cross-section through the inward displacement of its upper and lower radial extrema relative to the geometric center. It characterizes the complete boundary rather than either half-plane extremum alone.

For the upper and lower boundary extrema, the aggregate triangularity is defined as

$$
\delta = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{R_0-R_u}{a}+\frac{R_0-R_l}{a}\right)
$$

where $\delta$ is the plasma-boundary triangularity, $R_0$ is the major-radius coordinate of the geometric center, $R_u$ and $R_l$ are the major-radius coordinates of the upper and lower boundary extrema, and $a$ is the boundary minor radius. The coordinates refer to the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity applies to the entire plasma boundary and aggregates the upper and lower extremal displacements into one shape parameter. It excludes the separately resolved [upper triangularity of the plasma boundary](name:upper_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary) and [lower triangularity of the plasma boundary](name:lower_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary), which retain only one extremum. It also differs from [triangularity of a flux surface](name:triangularity_of_flux_surface), which describes an individual nested magnetic flux surface rather than the outer plasma boundary.
enclosing_statements: Description of the plasma boundary used by fixed-boundary codes and typically chosen at psi_norm = 99.x% of the separatrix

definition: Plasma current (Ip) is the net signed conventional electric current flowing toroidally through the plasma column, expressed in A. It is the integral of the toroidal plasma current density over a complete poloidal cross-section, with opposing contributions combined algebraically. Positive current is anti-clockwise when viewed from above. Values may be obtained from magnetic measurements or calculated from a reconstructed equilibrium; the fibre-optic current sensor reports the total toroidal current through the area outlined by its fibre path, measured using the Faraday magneto-optic effect. Unlike population-resolved or flux-surface-enclosed currents, the global plasma quantity includes all plasma charge carriers over the full cross-section.
documentation: This is the global toroidal current, not a local current density, a field-parallel current, a runaway-electron contribution, or the current assigned to a single plasma filament. A cumulative toroidal plasma current evaluated at the full plasma boundary recovers the global value. Measured and equilibrium-reconstructed values represent the same physical quantity obtained by different methods; magnetic estimates may provide several calculation methods, with the generally recommended method first. For fibre-optic measurements, the enclosing fibre path specifies the integration area, so the reported enclosed current must be interpreted with that measurement boundary in mind. Currents assigned to external coils or passive structures are distinct quantities.

definition: Minimum gas flow is the smallest pressure-volume gas throughput that a gas injection valve can reliably deliver, defining the lower bound of its controllable range.
documentation:
Minimum gas flow is the lower reliable operating limit of the pressure-volume throughput delivered by a gas injection valve. It identifies the smallest controllable value of the aggregate gas stream throughput, rather than a molecular-species flow or particle-number rate.

The pressure-volume throughput represented by this quantity is defined as

$$
Q_g = p_g \frac{dV_g}{dt}
$$

where $Q_g$ is gas pressure-volume throughput, $p_g$ is gas pressure at the flow boundary, $V_g$ is the volume of gas crossing that boundary, and $t$ is time.

This quantity applies to the aggregate gas stream delivered through an injection system across a defined flow boundary. The stream is not restricted to a particular molecular species or charge state, and this quantity is distinct from mass flow and particle-number rate. Its defining distinction is the lower reliable operating bound, rather than an unrestricted instantaneous throughput.

The gas flow quantity defines the same pressure-volume throughput without imposing a lower-limit condition; minimum gas flow is its lower reliable operating bound. Conversely, [maximum gas flow](name:maximum_gas_flow) is the upper reliable operating bound, so the two quantities delimit the controllable range rather than represent different throughput definitions.

definition: Vertical coordinate of the constraint position specifies its signed height from the zero-height plane, parallel to the symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
Vertical coordinate of the constraint position is its signed height relative to the zero-height plane in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height parallel to the toroidal symmetry axis.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
Z = \mathbf{x}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}}
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is the position vector of the constraint position measured from the coordinate origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the upward unit vector along the symmetry axis.

This quantity applies individually at each constraint position. It is a point coordinate, not a spatial average of position or the value of the constrained physical observable.

The same vertical projection defines the [vertical coordinate of a measurement position](name:vertical_coordinate_of_measurement_position), while this quantity is specifically evaluated at the constraint position.

Sign convention: Positive when the constraint position lies above the zero-height plane along the upward unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$.

definition: Cumulative equivalent-electron inventory of all gas species introduced by injection during the plasma prefill phase, summed over species.
documentation:
This quantity is the total gas inventory accumulated during the plasma prefill phase, expressed as an equivalent-electron count and summed over all injected species. It represents the integrated amount introduced before plasma breakdown, rather than an instantaneous injection rate.

The accumulated equivalent-electron count is defined by

$$
N_{\mathrm{eq}}(t) = \sum_s \int_{t_0}^{\mathrm{min}(t,t_1)} \dot{N}_{s,\mathrm{eq}}(t')\,dt'
$$

where $s$ indexes injected gas species, $\dot{N}_{s,\mathrm{eq}}$ is the equivalent-electron injection rate of species $s$, $t_0$ and $N_{\mathrm{eq}}(t)$ is the equivalent-electron count of species $s$, $t_0$ and $t_1$ delimit the prefill phase, and $t$ is the evaluation time. The sum includes all species; a species-specific quantity such as [accumulated hydrogen prefill count](name:accumulated_hydrogen_prefill_count) is a component of this total. The quantity is distinct from the instantaneous injection rate and from inventories restricted to one species, while [accumulated prefill gas count](name:accumulated_prefill_gas_count) denotes the near-equivalent total inventory.
name: accumulated_total_prefill_gas_equivalent_electron_count

definition: Signed toroidal component of the equilibrium magnetic field at the designated reference point whose major radius is the reference major radius. It is obtained as B_phi,ref = B_eq(x_ref) · e_phi(x_ref), where e_phi points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle phi in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. Positive values indicate that direction. The quantity is supplied as a dimensional normalization reference for local gyrokinetic calculations and is expressed in T.
documentation: This scalar is the reference-location specialization of toroidal magnetic field and the toroidal projection of the reference magnetic-field vector, rather than its magnitude. The full reference point specifies the evaluation location; its major radius alone does not generally determine the field. For an axisymmetric equilibrium, the value is independent of the reference toroidal angle. The reference location need not be the magnetic axis or a specified flux-surface location. Unlike toroidal vacuum magnetic field, this quantity is not restricted to the external-current contribution. Its role in normalization does not make it dimensionless or imply an average.
enclosing_statements: Physical quantities used for normalization (useful to link to the original simulation/experience)
name: toroidal_reference_magnetic_field
source_descriptions: Toroidal magnetic field at major radius r

definition: Length of the minor oblique parallelogram side of a plasma-filament element, inclined at angle beta to the vertical height axis.
documentation:
The minor oblique parallelogram-side length of a plasma-filament element is the Euclidean length of the side inclined at angle beta to the vertical height direction. It characterizes one side of the element's oblique cross-sectional geometry.

The side length is defined by the separation of its two endpoints:

$$
\ell_\beta = \left\lVert \mathbf{x}_{\beta,2} - \mathbf{x}_{\beta,1} \right\rVert
$$

where $\ell_\beta$ is the minor side length, $\mathbf{x}_{\beta,1}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{\beta,2}$ are the position vectors of its endpoints, and $\lVert\cdot\rVert$ denotes the Euclidean norm. The inclination angle $\beta$ is measured relative to the vertical height direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies to one discrete plasma current-carrying filament element and is neither summed nor averaged over elements. It excludes the complementary major oblique side and therefore is distinct from [major length of the plasma filament](name:major_length_of_plasma_filament).

This quantity specializes length of the plasma filament by selecting its minor, beta-inclined side. The paired major-length quantity selects the complementary oblique side of the same element.
name: minor_length_of_plasma_filament

definition: Complex scalar E-minus coefficient of a coherent electromagnetic-wave electric field, transverse to the static magnetic field, given on grid subsets and retaining the amplitude and phase of its right-hand circular polarization.
documentation: The right-hand circularly polarized wave electric field is the E-minus polarization contribution of the complex [wave electric field](name:wave_electric_field), perpendicular to the local static magnetic field. It retains the local amplitude and phase of that circular-polarization contribution. It is a scalar value provided per element in the grid subset.
enclosing_statements: Components of the wave electric field
Solution by a full wave code, given on a generic grid description, for various time slices
Wave description for each frequency

Right hand circularly polarised component of the perpendicular (to the static magnetic field) electric field, given on various grid subsets Right-hand circularly polarised component (E−) of the wave electric field perpendicular to the static magnetic field, given on GGD grid subsets. This component drives ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH) and is key to wave-particle coupling.
name: right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field
source_descriptions: Right hand circularly polarised component of the perpendicular (to the static magnetic field) electric field, given on various grid subsets
One scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.

definition: Length of the minor, beta-inclined side of a plasma-filament element's poloidal parallelogram cross-section, obtained as the Euclidean distance between the side's endpoints and expressed in m. The angle beta is measured relative to the vertical height axis Z in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. The quantity describes one element, without summation or averaging, and excludes the complementary major, alpha-inclined side.
documentation: This scalar specifies the minor oblique side of a single plasma current-carrying filament element. For endpoint position vectors x_beta,1 and x_beta,2, its value is ell_beta = ||x_beta,2 - x_beta,1||, where the norm is the Euclidean norm. It is a straight cross-sectional side length, not a magnetic-field-line length, a filament trajectory length, or a cross-sectional area. The major-side length selects the complementary side inclined relative to the major-radius axis. The neighbouring second_inclination_length_of_plasma_filament describes the same beta-inclined side; the supplied descriptions establish no physical distinction between those two labels.
name: minor_length_of_plasma_filament

definition: Reciprocal square of total magnetic-field strength in an equilibrium plasma, evaluated locally using all vector components, without restriction to a particle population and with no flux-surface or volume aggregation, providing a positive magnetic-geometry factor for equilibrium and flux-surface-averaged transport relations. Its unit is T^-2.
documentation:
The inverse square of total magnetic-field strength is a local magnetic-geometry factor that increases as the total field weakens and remains positive wherever the field magnitude is nonzero.

It is defined as the reciprocal of the [square of magnetic-field magnitude](name:square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude):

$$
B^{-2} = \frac{1}{B^2} = \frac{1}{\lvert \mathbf{B} \rvert^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic-field vector and $B$ is its magnitude.

The quantity applies to the full magnetic field in an equilibrium plasma, including all vector components and without restriction to a particle population. At the parent level it is a local quantity with no flux-surface or volume aggregation; it is distinct from the squared field magnitude itself and from the reciprocal square of any selected field component.

The [flux-surface-averaged inverse square of magnetic-field magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude) is obtained by applying a flux-surface average to this local factor. The averaging is a separate aggregation operation and does not alter the reciprocal-square transformation.
name: inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude

definition: Vertical coordinate Z of a grid location, expressed in m in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, with the vertical direction parallel to the toroidal symmetry axis. The value gives the height of the grid location, rather than a radial coordinate or an angular coordinate.
documentation: These values describe the vertical geometry of computational grids, including the non-axisymmetric magnetic-field map grid, equilibrium and vacuum-mode flux-surface coordinate grids, and equilibrium generic-grid subsets. The flux-surface coordinate grids store height on a square grid of flux and poloidal angle; the generic-grid representation provides one scalar height per grid-subset element. The quantity describes grid locations, not the position of a camera, measurement point, vessel, or other physical component, and does not denote the height of a coordinate-system origin.

definition: Dimensionless ratio of the collision frequency between a pair of particle species a and b to a characteristic transit angular frequency.
documentation:
This collisionality measures the strength of interspecies collisional relaxation between pairs of particle species relative to collisionless motion along magnetic-field trajectories.

$$\nu_{ab}^{*} = \frac{\nu_{ab}}{\omega_{\mathrm{char}}}$$

where $\nu_{ab}$ is the collision frequency between species $a$ and $b$, and $\omega_{\mathrm{char}}$ is the characteristic transit angular frequency; both quantities have reciprocal-time units.

The denominator is the characteristic transit frequency, not a streaming or bounce frequency, so this quantity is distinct from the collision frequency itself. It generalizes the population-specific electron collisionality and complements collisionality at the pedestal top when the characteristic frequency is evaluated there.
enclosing_statements: Collisions related quantities
name: normalized_interspecies_collisionality
source_descriptions: Normalised collisionality between two species

definition: Toroidal angle locating each point of a control surface about the machine symmetry axis, measured in the right-handed cylindrical frame from the facility-defined zero direction.
documentation:
The toroidal angle identifies the azimuthal location of a point on the control surface about the machine symmetry axis. It is the geometrical coordinate defined for [toroidal angle](name:toroidal_angle), with the control-surface locus providing the points to which it applies.

For a point with Cartesian coordinates $x$ and $y$ in the right-handed $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis, the angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame is defined by:

$$
\phi = \operatorname{atan2}(y,x) \pmod{2\pi}
$$

where $R$ is the major radius, $Z$ is vertical height, and the zero of $\phi$ follows the facility-defined reference direction. The angle is periodic, so values differing by an integer multiple of $2\pi$ represent the same toroidal direction; it is distinct from the vertical coordinate of the control surface.

Sign convention: Positive when $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above the $+\hat{Z}$ direction.
enclosing_statements: Magnetic field components and Fourier decomposition of the normal components of the magnetic field for a set of given control surfaces
Set of time slices
name: toroidal_angle_of_control_surface
source_descriptions: Toroidal angle array, on which the Fourier decomposition is carried out

definition: Major-radius coordinate of a magnetic flux surface at its inboard midplane intersection, locating the high-field-side point relative to the toroidal symmetry axis.
documentation:
This quantity is the major-radius coordinate of the point where a magnetic flux surface intersects the inboard midplane, identifying the high-field-side location of that surface relative to the toroidal symmetry axis. It is a locus-specific form of the [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate).

For a magnetic flux surface $\mathcal{S}$, the inboard-midplane radial coordinate is defined by

$$
R_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S}) = R\!\left(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S})\right)
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S})$ is the quantity defined here, $R(\mathbf{x})$ is the major-radius coordinate of spatial position $\mathbf{x}$, $\mathcal{S}$ is the specified magnetic flux surface, and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathcal{S})$ is its inboard midplane intersection. The coordinates are expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The scope is one coordinate value for each specified magnetic flux surface at its inboard, high-field-side midplane intersection. It is not a flux-surface average, a poloidal or toroidal average, or the corresponding outboard-midplane coordinate; the latter is represented by [radial coordinate at outboard midplane](name:radial_coordinate_at_outboard_midplane). Unlike [radial magnetic field](name:radial_magnetic_field), this quantity describes the location of a surface and not a magnetic-field component.

This quantity specializes [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) by fixing the evaluation locus to the inboard midplane. Comparing it with the outboard-midplane value characterizes the horizontal extent and radial placement of the same magnetic flux surface.
enclosing_statements: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux
Set of equilibria at various time slices
name: radial_coordinate_at_inboard_midplane
source_descriptions: Radial coordinate (major radius) on the inboard side of the magnetic axis

definition: Dimensionless Luce (2013) squareness coefficient for the lower-inner, high-field-side quadrant of a nested magnetic flux surface, measuring signed departure from a reference ellipse. The reference ellipse is defined in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame and shares the surface's center, horizontal half-width, and elongation. Zero represents no additional lower-inner corner shaping; positive values indicate an outward, boxier corner and negative values an inward, more indented corner. This coefficient is not an average of the upper and lower inner coefficients. It is specified as a one-dimensional radial profile as a function of poloidal flux at each equilibrium time slice; its unit is 1.
documentation:
The lower-inner squareness of a flux surface is the dimensionless Luce (2013) shape coefficient that characterizes how the lower, high-field-side quadrant of a nested toroidal magnetic flux surface departs from a reference ellipse sharing the same center, horizontal half-width, and [elongation](name:elongation_of_flux_surface). It is the lower-quadrant component of [inner squareness of a flux surface](name:inner_squareness_of_flux_surface), complementary to [upper-inner squareness of a flux surface](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface).

The reference ellipse is parameterized in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame by

$$
\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{ref}}(\theta)=\left(R_0+a\cos\theta,\;Z_0+\kappa a\sin\theta\right)
$$

where $R$ is major radius, $Z$ is vertical height, $\theta$ is a poloidal parameter, $(R_0,Z_0)$ is the ellipse center, $a$ is its horizontal half-width, and $\kappa$ is its elongation. Within the Luce model, $\zeta_{\mathrm{li}}=0$ represents no additional lower-inner corner shaping; positive values indicate an outward, boxier corner and negative values an inward, more indented corner.

This coefficient describes only the lower high-field-side quadrant and is not an average of the upper and lower inner coefficients.
enclosing_statements: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux
Set of equilibria at various time slices
name: lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface
source_descriptions: Lower inner squareness (definition from T. Luce, Plasma Phys. Control. Fusion 55 (2013) 095009)

definition: Spectral photon radiance is the directional photon arrival rate from plasma emission per projected area, viewing solid angle, and wavelength interval.
documentation:
Spectral photon radiance describes the absolute photon-number brightness of plasma radiation along a specified viewing direction, resolved by wavelength. Its spectral dependence is expressed per wavelength interval, not per frequency or photon-energy interval.

The defining differential relation is:

$$
dN_{\gamma} = L_{\gamma}(\lambda)\,dt\,dA_{\perp}\,d\Omega\,d\lambda
$$

where $N_{\gamma}$ is the number of photons crossing a collecting surface, $L_{\gamma}(\lambda)$ is the spectral photon radiance at wavelength $\lambda$, $t$ is time, $A_{\perp}$ is the collecting surface's projected area perpendicular to the ray direction, and $\Omega$ is the solid angle about that direction.

The quantity includes the line and continuum contributions present at the specified wavelength without selecting a particular emitting species or radiation mechanism. It is not a local volumetric photon-production rate, an electromagnetic energy radiance, or a detector count rate.

Integrating the contribution from an identified transition over its wavelength interval gives the [photon radiance at a spectral line](name:photon_radiance_at_spectral_line), rather than a wavelength-resolved radiance density. The [spectral bremsstrahlung photon radiance](name:spectral_bremsstrahlung_photon_radiance) is the contribution restricted to free-free emission.
enclosing_statements: Set of spectra obtained by various gratings
Set of channels (lines-of-sight). The line-of-sight is defined by the centre of the collimating aperture and the position of the measurements.
Set of channels (detector or pixel of a camera)
Quantities measured by the channel if connected to a grating spectrometer
name: spectral_photon_radiance
source_descriptions: Calibrated spectral radiance (radiance per unit wavelength)

definition: Radial derivative dV/dρ_tor of the cumulative volume V enclosed by a nested magnetic flux surface with respect to its dimensionful toroidal-flux coordinate ρ_tor, with time and other independent coordinates held fixed. The coordinate has unit m, so the derivative has unit m^2.
documentation: The enclosed volume is accumulated from the magnetic axis to the selected flux surface, rather than being the volume of a finite shell. This quantity gives the volume increment per increment of the dimensionful toroidal-flux coordinate: dV = (dV/dρ_tor)dρ_tor. It is positive on regular nested surfaces when ρ_tor increases outward. It is distinct from the enclosed volume itself, its derivative with respect to poloidal magnetic flux, the corresponding derivative of enclosed poloidal cross-sectional area, and the temporal derivative of this volume derivative. It is a geometric quantity with no species weighting.
enclosing_statements: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux
Set of equilibria at various time slices
name: derivative_of_volume_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate
