definition: Flux-surface-averaged rate of Coulomb-collisional energy transfer per unit volume from co-passing fast particles to fast ions of one specified species and charge state.
documentation:
Co-passing fast-ion charge-state collisional power density is the signed volumetric rate of kinetic-energy transfer from the co-passing part of a fast-particle distribution to fast ions of one specified species and charge state, averaged over a magnetic flux surface. The co-passing restriction selects the donating particles' passing guiding-center orbits, not the recipient ions' orbit class.

The defining kinetic-energy moment is

$$
P_{i,q}^{\mathrm{co}\to\mathrm{fast}} = \left\langle \int \frac{1}{2}m_i v^2 C_{i,q}^{\mathrm{coll}}\!\left[f_{i,q}^{\mathrm{fast}},f_{\mathrm{co}}^{\mathrm{fast}}\right] \, d^3v \right\rangle_{\psi}
$$

where $P_{i,q}^{\mathrm{co}\to\mathrm{fast}}$ is this power density, $i$ identifies the recipient ion species, $q$ is its specified ionic charge number, $m_i$ is its ion mass, $v$ is the recipient speed, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. The distribution $f_{i,q}^{\mathrm{fast}}$ describes the recipient fast ions, while $f_{\mathrm{co}}^{\mathrm{fast}}$ describes the co-passing fast-particle donors. The operator $C_{i,q}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ gives the collisional time derivative of the recipient distribution due to those donors. The brackets denote the volume-shell-weighted magnetic flux-surface average, with $\psi$ labeling the surface.

Only the specified recipient species and charge state are included; no recipient-species or charge-state sum is implied. Counter-passing and trapped donors are excluded. Unlike [co-passing thermal-ion charge-state collisional power density](name:co_passing_thermal_power_density_due_to_coulomb_collisions_with_ion_state), this quantity concerns fast rather than thermal recipient ions. It is an energy-exchange rate, not stored kinetic-energy density or volume-integrated power.

Summing over all ionic charge states of the same recipient species gives [co-passing fast-ion collisional power density](name:co_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions). Its relationship to the all-orbit parent, [fast-ion charge-state collisional power density](name:fast_ion_charge_state_power_density_due_to_collisions), is an aggregation over co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped donors with the same recipient population and transfer direction. Transfer from a bulk-ion charge state to a fast-particle distribution is a different exchange and must not be substituted for the fast-to-fast transfer defined here.

Sign convention: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy from the co-passing fast-particle distribution to the specified fast-ion charge-state population; negative when the net transfer is reversed.

definition: Number density of tungsten ions, obtained by summing the number densities of all positive tungsten charge states: n_W = sum from Z = 1 to 74 of n_W^(Z+). Each ion is counted once, without charge weighting, and neutral tungsten is excluded. The quantity may be evaluated locally or spatially averaged over a specified domain; no particular locus or averaging operation is prescribed. Its unit is m^-3.
documentation: Tungsten density describes the concentration of positively charged tungsten ions rather than neutral tungsten, a single charge-state population, or a tungsten-to-electron density ratio. Unlike the volume-averaged, line-averaged and locus-specific tungsten-density quantities, this general quantity does not prescribe an averaging domain or evaluation location. Any spatial average must specify its domain and averaging convention while retaining the sum over positive charge states.
name: tungsten_density

definition: Characteristic timescale of electric-current decrease during a disruption, defined by a specified linear-threshold or exponential decay convention.
documentation:
This quantity characterizes electric-current decay during a disruption. It encompasses the total plasma current and the current carried by a specified particle population, without imposing a particular current component or decay convention.

For a linear threshold convention, the extrapolated full-decay time is defined by:

$$
\tau_{\mathrm{lin}}=\frac{t(f_{\mathrm{low}})-t(f_{\mathrm{high}})}{f_{\mathrm{high}}-f_{\mathrm{low}}}
$$

where $\tau_{\mathrm{lin}}$ is the linear decay time, $f_{\mathrm{high}}$ and $f_{\mathrm{low}}$ are the upper and lower fractions of a specified reference current magnitude, and $t(f)$ is the time at which the decaying current magnitude reaches fraction $f$ of that reference.

An exponential convention instead defines an e-folding time through $I(t)=I_0\exp[-(t-t_0)/\tau_{\mathrm{exp}}]$, where $I(t)$ is the selected current magnitude at time $t$, $I_0$ is its value at reference time $t_0$, and $\tau_{\mathrm{exp}}$ is the exponential decay time. A linear threshold time is not generally equal to an exponential e-folding time.

The [plasma-current decay time](name:plasma_decay_time_due_to_disruption) uses the linear construction with upper and lower fractions of 0.8 and 0.2. The [runaway-electron current decay time](name:runaway_electron_decay_time_due_to_disruption) applies to the total toroidal runaway-electron current and permits custom linear, fixed 20–80% linear, or exponential conventions. These specializations characterize different current populations and need not have equal decay times; neither denotes a local current-density decay time or an electron-temperature decay time.
name: decay_time_due_to_disruption

definition: Local number density of hydrogen ions (H+) in the scrape-off-layer plasma immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing limiter surface, expressed in m^-3. It counts hydrogen ions per unit physical volume, excluding neutral hydrogen, deuterium, tritium and other species. The precise plasma evaluation point relative to the presheath or sheath entrance is not specified by the source.
documentation: This is the hydrogen-specific component of density_at_limiter, provided in the source's species-resolved ion-density summary. It distinguishes hydrogen ions from electrons and other ion species at the same limiter location. The limiter locus distinguishes it from hydrogen density evaluated on the last closed magnetic flux surface or at a divertor target; it does not denote the separatrix–limiter contact point or a distribution along the limiter surface. The source specifies neither a measurement or calculation method nor a more precise evaluation point.

Ion density per species Ion number density (ni) resolved by species at the limiter location. Provides species-resolved ion densities at the plasma boundary as part of the limiter parameter summary.
Parameters at the limiter
Plasma parameter values at different locations

definition: Area enclosed by the last closed magnetic flux surface in a poloidal plane, defining the equilibrium plasma cross-sectional size at the plasma boundary.
documentation:
This quantity is the geometric area enclosed by the last closed magnetic flux surface (LCFS), which forms the plasma boundary, in a poloidal cross-section.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the enclosed area is defined by

$$
A_{\rm LCFS} = \iint_{\mathcal{S}_{\rm LCFS}} dR\,dZ
$$

where $A_{\rm LCFS}$ is the LCFS cross-sectional area, $\mathcal{S}_{\rm LCFS}$ is the region enclosed by the LCFS contour at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical height, and $dR\,dZ$ is the poloidal-plane area element.

This is a global equilibrium quantity for the complete plasma-boundary contour. It is not a local surface element, a flux-surface average, or the area of a toroidal surface formed by revolving the contour.

It is the plasma-boundary specialization of [poloidal plane cross-sectional area of a flux surface](name:poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_flux_surface), whose corresponding area is defined for an arbitrary closed magnetic flux surface; the LCFS is the outermost such surface enclosing the plasma.
enclosing_statements: 0D parameters of the equilibrium
Set of equilibria at various time slices

source_descriptions: Area of the LCFS poloidal cross section

definition: Ratio of the squared gradient magnitude of the length-valued toroidal-flux coordinate to squared major radius, defining a local equilibrium metric coefficient.
documentation:
Ratio of the squared toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient magnitude to squared major radius is a local equilibrium metric coefficient. It encodes flux-surface spacing with inverse-square major-radius weighting.

The defining relation is:

$$
G = \frac{|\nabla \rho_{\mathrm{tor}}|^2}{R^2}
$$

where $G$ is this local coefficient, $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the length-valued toroidal-flux coordinate, and $\nabla$ is the spatial gradient operator. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is the distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the vertical height.

The toroidal-flux coordinate retains its prescribed scale; no boundary normalization or substitution of an arbitrary flux label is implied. The denominator is squared major radius, not its inverse. The squared gradient magnitude distinguishes this coefficient from inverse squared major radius alone.

This quantity is a pointwise ratio without spatial averaging. Its flux-surface-averaged counterpart averages the complete ratio over a closed magnetic flux surface; it is not the ratio of separately averaged numerator and denominator.

$$a/b$$

The magnitude is the Euclidean norm of a vector quantity, or the modulus of a complex one.

The ratio is one quantity divided by another.

The square is a scalar quantity multiplied by itself, or a vector's dot product with itself.
name: ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_major_radius

definition: The signed y component of the unit vector along the major axis of an elliptic shatter cone is its projection in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.
documentation:
The signed y component of the unit vector along the major axis of an elliptic shatter cone is the projection of that major-axis direction onto the $y$ basis direction of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame. The major-axis direction is the orientation of the principal semiaxis of the cone's elliptic cross-section.

The component is defined by

$$
e_{\mathrm{maj},y} = \hat{e}_{\mathrm{maj}} \cdot \hat{y}
$$

where $e_{\mathrm{maj},y}$ is the y component of the shatter-cone major-axis unit vector, $\hat{e}_{\mathrm{maj}}$ is the unit vector along the major axis of the elliptic shatter cone, and $\hat{y}$ is the y basis vector of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame.

This quantity applies to the geometry of an elliptic shatter cone and to the major semiaxis orientation of its elliptic cross-section; its aggregation convention is none, because it is a single vector component rather than a sum or mean. It is distinct from the unsigned major-axis length, from the [y component of the shatter-cone direction unit vector](name:y_direction_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone), which describes the cone direction rather than the major-axis orientation, and from the [y component of the minor-axis unit vector](name:y_minor_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone), which refers to the orthogonal minor semiaxis.

Together with the [x component](name:x_major_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone) and [z component](name:z_major_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone), this quantity forms the Cartesian representation of $\hat{e}_{\mathrm{maj}}$; the linked x and z components and $e_{\mathrm{maj},y}$ satisfy $(e_{\mathrm{maj},x})^2 + (e_{\mathrm{maj},y})^2 + (e_{\mathrm{maj},z})^2 = 1$, where $e_{\mathrm{maj},x}$ and $e_{\mathrm{maj},z}$ are the linked x and z components. The major-axis and minor-axis unit vectors jointly orient the elliptic cone and satisfy $\hat{e}_{\mathrm{maj}} \cdot \hat{e}_{\mathrm{min}} = 0$, where $\hat{e}_{\mathrm{min}}$ is the minor-axis unit vector with [x](name:x_minor_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone), [y](name:y_minor_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone), and [z](name:z_minor_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone) components.

Sign convention: Positive when $\hat{e}_{\mathrm{maj}}$ has a component in the $+\hat{y}$ direction of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame.

definition: Dimensionless factor controlling the relative contribution of an interferometer beam’s line-integrated electron-density residual to an equilibrium objective function.
documentation:
The equilibrium weight assigned to an interferometer-beam constraint is a nonnegative factor that sets the relative importance of its line-integrated electron-density residual in an equilibrium objective function. It applies to the constraint associated with one interferometer beam rather than to the electron density itself.

A weighted least-squares objective containing this constraint is defined by

$$
J = \frac{1}{2} \sum_i w_i^2 \left(\frac{y_i^{\mathrm{rec}} - y_i^{\mathrm{meas}}}{\sigma_i}\right)^2
$$

where $J$ is the equilibrium objective function, $i$ indexes individual constraints, $w_i$ is the equilibrium weight, $y_i^{\mathrm{rec}}$ is the reconstructed line-integrated electron density for constraint $i$, $y_i^{\mathrm{meas}}$ is its measured line-integrated electron density, and $\sigma_i$ is the standard deviation assigned to its measurement error.

For this quantity, $i$ denotes an interferometer-beam line-integrated electron-density constraint. The weight is specific to that individual constraint; the objective function aggregates all constraint contributions through the summation. It is not the line-integrated electron density, either its measured or reconstructed value, and it is distinct from the [calibration coefficient of an interferometer beam](name:spectral_calibration_factor_at_line_of_sight), which characterizes signal calibration rather than equilibrium-objective weighting.

This quantity has the same objective-function role as the equilibrium weight of a flux loop and the equilibrium weight of a poloidal magnetic-field probe; those related weights differ by the physical measurement constraint to which they apply.
enclosing_statements: Set of line integrated density measurements Set of line-integrated electron density (∫ne·dl) measurements used as constraints in equilibrium reconstruction. Each entry stores measured, reconstructed, and chi-squared values quantifying the fit quality.

In case of equilibrium reconstruction under constraints, measurements used to constrain the equilibrium, reconstructed values and accuracy of the fit. The names of the child nodes correspond to the following definition: the solver aims at minimizing a cost function defined as : J=1/2*sum_i [ weight_i^2 (reconstructed_i - measured_i)^2 / sigma_i^2 ]. in which sigma_i is the standard deviation of the measurement error (to be found in the IDS of the measurement)
Set of equilibria at various time slices

source_descriptions: Weight given to the measurement

definition: Lower-bound photon energy sets the low-energy cutoff for X-ray photon counting, admitting only photons above the threshold of the specified detector pixel or channel.
documentation:
Lower-bound photon energy is the low-energy edge of an X-ray detection or emission band. For photon counting, it is the threshold that an incident photon must exceed to be eligible for registration.

The lower-threshold requirement for counting is:

$$
E_{\gamma} > E_{\gamma,\min}
$$

where $E_{\gamma}$ is the incident photon energy and $E_{\gamma,\min}$ is the lower photon-energy threshold assigned to the specified detector pixel or channel.

The counting threshold applies individually to that pixel or channel, rather than representing an average over the detector. For an energy-resolved emission band, the bound instead specifies the low-energy boundary of the included emission.

Together with [upper photon energy](name:upper_photon_energy), this bound specifies the spectral window. It is a band boundary, not a [central or representative pixel photon energy](name:energy_of_detector_pixel). Exceeding the lower threshold is necessary for counting but does not imply unit detection probability.
enclosing_statements: Set of energy bands in which photons are counted by the detector Array of energy bands in which hard X-ray (HXR) photons are counted by each detector channel. Each band is defined by lower and upper energy bounds and an associated detection efficiency, enabling spectrally resolved measurements.
Set of channels (detector or pixel of a camera)
Emissivity profile per energy band (assumed common to all channels used in the profile reconstruction)

Set of energy bands in which photons are counted by the detector Set of energy bands defining the spectral sensitivity windows for a soft X-ray (SXR) detector channel. Each band is characterized by lower and upper energy bounds and detection efficiency as a function of photon energy.
name: lower_bound_photon_energy
source_descriptions: Lower energy detection threshold on each pixel of the detector (photons are counted only if their energy is above this value)

definition: Toroidal total current density is the net conventional charge flux per unit area around the symmetry axis, formed by algebraically summing all included current contributions.
documentation:
Toroidal total current density is the signed local projection of the net [current density](name:current_density) onto the toroidal direction. It combines all included contributions before or after projection onto that same direction.

The projection and aggregation are defined by:

$$
j_\phi = \hat{\phi}\cdot\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{tot}} = \sum_k \hat{\phi}\cdot\mathbf{j}_k
$$

where $j_\phi$ is the toroidal total current density, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total current-density vector, $\mathbf{j}_k$ is an included current-density contribution, and $k$ labels those contributions. The unit vector $\hat{\phi}$ points toward increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The total is an algebraic sum, not a sum of magnitudes, and does not select a particular species, charge state, or current-generation mechanism. The quantity is local, with no restriction to a particular plasma region; it is neither a current-density magnitude nor a flux-surface average or spatially integrated current.

This quantity specializes [total current density](name:total_current_density) by fixing its common signed projection to the toroidal direction. The adjacent [radial total current density](name:radial_total_current_density) instead projects the same net charge-flux density onto the outward major-radius direction.

Sign convention: Positive when the net conventional charge transport is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle, counterclockwise when viewed from above along the negative vertical direction.

definition: Length of the minor oblique parallelogram side of a plasma-filament element, inclined at angle beta to the vertical height axis. The length is the Euclidean norm of the separation of the side's two endpoints in the element's poloidal parallelogram cross-section. The inclination angle beta is measured relative to the vertical height direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where R is major radius, phi is toroidal angle, and Z is vertical height. The quantity applies to one discrete plasma current-carrying filament element and is neither summed nor averaged over elements. It excludes the complementary major oblique side. Its unit is m.
documentation:
The minor oblique parallelogram-side length of a plasma-filament element is the Euclidean length of the side inclined at angle beta to the vertical height direction. It characterizes one side of the element's oblique cross-sectional geometry.

The side length is defined by the separation of its two endpoints:

$$
\ell_\beta = \left\lVert \mathbf{x}_{\beta,2} - \mathbf{x}_{\beta,1} \right\rVert
$$

where $\ell_\beta$ is the minor side length, $\mathbf{x}_{\beta,1}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{\beta,2}$ are the position vectors of its endpoints, and $\lVert\cdot\rVert$ denotes the Euclidean norm. The inclination angle $\beta$ is measured relative to the vertical height direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity applies to one discrete plasma current-carrying filament element and is neither summed nor averaged over elements. It excludes the complementary major oblique side and therefore is distinct from [major length of the plasma filament](name:major_length_of_plasma_filament).

This quantity specializes length of the plasma filament by selecting its minor, beta-inclined side. The paired major-length quantity selects the complementary oblique side of the same element.
name: minor_length_of_plasma_filament

definition: Vertical coordinate of the constraint position specifies its signed height from the zero-height plane, parallel to the symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. It is evaluated for each equilibrium time slice and expressed in metres.
documentation:
Vertical coordinate of the constraint position is its signed height relative to the zero-height plane in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height parallel to the toroidal symmetry axis.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
Z = \mathbf{x}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}}
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is the position vector of the constraint position measured from the coordinate origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the upward unit vector along the symmetry axis.

This quantity applies individually at each constraint position. It is a point coordinate, not a spatial average of position or the value of the constrained physical observable.

The same vertical projection defines the [vertical coordinate of a measurement position](name:vertical_coordinate_of_measurement_position), while this quantity is specifically evaluated at the constraint position.

Sign convention: Positive when the constraint position lies above the zero-height plane along the upward unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$.

definition: Rate at which particles represented as equivalent electrons are removed from the plasma region by wall pumping, giving global electron-equivalent exhaust throughput.
documentation:
The rate at which particles of the electron-equivalent population are removed from the plasma region by wall pumping is the global scalar representation of the wall particle-removal flux. It describes pumped particle exhaust using equivalent-electron counting rather than a local wall flux density.

The global removal rate is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{e,\mathrm{pump}} = \frac{dN_{e,\mathrm{removed}}}{dt}
$$

where $\Gamma_{e,\mathrm{pump}}$ is the pumped particle-removal rate expressed in equivalent electrons, $N_{e,\mathrm{removed}}$ is the cumulative number of electron equivalents removed by wall pumping, and $t$ is time.

This quantity is aggregated over the wall and represents the total pumping throughput for the electron-equivalent population. The electron-equivalent basis does not assert that all removed particles are physical electrons, and the quantity is not an areal flux density, an electrical current, or a rate for one specified neutral species.

It is the electron-specific specialization of the general [particle-removal flux at the wall due to pumping](name:particle_rate_at_wall_due_to_pumping). In contrast, [neutral particle flux at the wall due to pumping](name:neutral_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_pumping) uses a specified neutral species as its counting population rather than equivalent-electron counting.
name: electron_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_pumping

definition: Radial flux-surface location of the selected plasma boundary at a given equilibrium time slice, expressed by the normalized poloidal flux coordinate. It is the linear normalized poloidal flux value, increasing from zero at the magnetic axis to one at the separatrix, of the closed flux surface taken as the plasma boundary; fixed-boundary equilibrium calculations commonly set it slightly below one (typically 99.x%) to select a surface just inside the separatrix. It is dimensionless, with unit 1.
documentation:
The normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the plasma boundary is the value of the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate) on the closed flux surface selected as the plasma boundary. It is the linear normalized poloidal flux, labeling the boundary's radial position between the magnetic axis and the last closed flux surface.

Its value is the poloidal flux difference from the magnetic axis normalized to the axis-to-separatrix flux difference:

$$
\psi_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{boundary}} = \frac{\psi_{\mathrm{boundary}} - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}{\psi_{\mathrm{sep}} - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}
$$

where $\psi_{\mathrm{boundary}}$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) on the selected plasma-boundary surface, $\psi_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the [poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis), and $\psi_{\mathrm{sep}}$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at the separatrix (last closed flux surface).

The label equals zero at the magnetic axis and equals one when the selected plasma boundary coincides with the separatrix; a value below one selects an internal closed flux surface. Its defining role is to specify, for fixed-boundary equilibrium representations, which closed flux surface is taken as the plasma boundary, commonly a surface just inside the separatrix so that the boundary remains strictly closed.

This is the linear normalized poloidal flux value itself, not its square root, and it is a flux-surface label rather than a signed poloidal-flux value or a geometric minor-radius measure. It is distinct from the toroidal-flux-based boundary label normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the plasma boundary, and it belongs to the same locus-valued family as the normalized poloidal flux coordinate at minimum safety factor and the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the pedestal](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_pedestal).
enclosing_statements: Description of the plasma boundary used by fixed-boundary codes and typically chosen at psi_norm = 99.x% of the separatrix
Set of equilibria at various time slices
name: normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary
source_descriptions: Value of the normalised poloidal flux at which the boundary is taken (typically 99.x %), the flux being normalised to its value at the separatrix

definition: Signed vertical position of the plasma-current centroid, obtained by weighting the toroidal current distribution by height in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
documentation:
The vertical coordinate of the plasma-current center is the current-density-weighted centroid height of the plasma current distribution in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

$$
Z_{\mathrm{c}} = \frac{\int_{\mathcal{A}} Z\,j_{\phi}(R,Z)\,dA}{\int_{\mathcal{A}} j_{\phi}(R,Z)\,dA}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{c}}$ and $Z$ are vertical coordinates in m, $R$ is major radius in m, $j_{\phi}$ is toroidal current density in A m$^{-2}$, $dA$ is differential poloidal cross-sectional area in m$^{2}$, and $\mathcal{A}$ is the region carrying plasma current. The current-weighted center is distinct from the geometric axis; its radial counterpart is the [radial coordinate of the current center](name:radial_coordinate_of_current_center).

Sign convention: Positive when the plasma-current centroid lies in the $+Z$ direction from the coordinate origin.
enclosing_statements: Position and vertical velocity of the current centre
0D parameters of the equilibrium
Set of equilibria at various time slices

source_descriptions: Height of the current center, defined as integral over the poloidal cross section of (j_tor*z*dS) / Ip

definition: Geometric rate at which the cumulative volume enclosed by a nested magnetic flux surface changes with its dimensionful toroidal-flux coordinate.
documentation:
This quantity is the geometric derivative of the cumulative volume enclosed by a nested magnetic flux surface with respect to the dimensionful toroidal-flux coordinate. It describes how rapidly the enclosed region expands as the flux-surface label changes.

The defining relation is

$$
\frac{dV}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}}
$$

where $V$ is the [volume enclosed by a flux surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface) and $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the dimensionful toroidal-flux coordinate labeling the nested surfaces.

The quantity applies to the three-dimensional region inside each selected nested magnetic flux surface. The volume is cumulative, beginning at the magnetic axis and extending to the specified surface; this is not a local plasma-population quantity and carries no species weighting. It is the derivative with respect to the toroidal-flux coordinate, not the volume itself or the derivative of the enclosed poloidal area.

As the derivative of [volume enclosed by a flux surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface), it provides the volume increment associated with a change in toroidal-flux coordinate and serves as a geometric coefficient in flux-surface-averaged transport relations. The derivative of area with respect to the toroidal-flux coordinate is the analogous area derivative, while [the temporal derivative of this volume derivative](name:time_derivative_of_derivative_of_volume_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate) describes its change in time.
enclosing_statements: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux
Set of equilibria at various time slices

The coordinates and reference length are expressed in m, giving unit 1. This label measures normalized geometric half-width, not normalized toroidal or poloidal magnetic flux.

Its value depends on the chosen reference length and is not necessarily one at the plasma boundary. Unlike normalized toroidal and poloidal flux coordinates, it is calculated from surface geometry rather than enclosed magnetic flux; unlike elongation, it describes normalized radial size rather than the ratio of vertical to radial extent.

definition: Global rate at which wall pumping removes particles from the plasma, counted in equivalent electrons rather than necessarily as physical electrons. The rate is aggregated over the wall and is dN_e,removed/dt, where N_e,removed is the cumulative number of electron equivalents removed by pumping. Its unit is s^-1.
documentation: This scalar quantity describes electron-equivalent exhaust throughput due to wall pumping. Equivalent-electron counting is the reporting convention and does not imply that the pumped particles are physical electrons. Unlike a local electron particle flux, this quantity is a wall-aggregated removal rate, not a rate per unit area or an electrical current. Unlike neutral particle flux at the wall due to pumping, it is not the particle-number throughput of one specified neutral species. It describes removal by pumping rather than particle return through recycling or surface emission.

definition: Spectral photon radiance is the calibrated directional photon arrival rate from plasma emission per projected collecting area, viewing solid angle, and wavelength interval. It is defined by dN_gamma = L_gamma(lambda) dt dA_perp dOmega dlambda, where A_perp is the collecting area projected perpendicular to the ray direction. It is expressed per unit wavelength, not per frequency or photon-energy interval, in m^-3.s^-1.sr^-1.
documentation: This quantity describes the absolute photon-number brightness of plasma radiation along a specified viewing direction, resolved by wavelength. It includes the line and continuum contributions present at that wavelength without restriction to an emitting species or radiation mechanism; spectral bremsstrahlung photon radiance instead selects only the free-free contribution. Unlike photon radiance at a spectral line, it is a wavelength-resolved density rather than a background-subtracted integral over an identified line. It is neither a local volumetric photon-production rate, an energy radiance, nor an uncalibrated detector count rate.

definition: Local particle number density of hydrogen ions in the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing limiter surface, evaluated on the plasma side of the magnetic presheath or documentation unchanged.
documentation:
Hydrogen density at a limiter is the local number density of hydrogen ions in the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing limiter surface. The evaluation point is on the plasma side of the magnetic presheath or sheath entrance; neutral hydrogen is excluded. For hydrogen, the charge-state sum reduces to the density of positively charged hydrogen ions, H+.

The local hydrogen-ion density is defined from the velocity distribution function:

$$
n_{\mathrm{H}^+} = \int f_{\mathrm{H}^+}(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{H}^+}$ is the hydrogen-ion number density, $f_{\mathrm{H}^+}$ is the hydrogen-ion velocity distribution function, and $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity at the evaluation point.

This quantity is the hydrogen-specific component of [density_at_limiter](name:density_at_limiter). It counts hydrogen ions separately from [deuterium_density_at_limiter](name:deuterium_density_at_limiter), and does not include neutral hydrogen or other ion species.
enclosing_statements: Hydrogen
Ion density per species Ion number density (ni) resolved by species at the limiter location. Provides species-resolved ion densities at the plasma boundary as part of the limiter parameter summary.
Parameters at the limiter
Plasma parameter values at different locations
name: hydrogen_density_at_limiter
source_descriptions: Value

definition: Minor radius of the plasma boundary is half the difference between the maximum and minimum major radii on its poloidal cross-sectional contour.
documentation:
Minor radius of the plasma boundary characterizes the horizontal size of its poloidal cross-section. It is a nonnegative geometric [radius](name:radius) defined by the contour's full major-radius extent.

The defining relation is

$$
R_{\mathrm{minor}} = \frac{R_{\max}-R_{\min}}{2}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{minor}}$ is the minor radius of the plasma boundary, and $R_{\max}$ and $R_{\min}$ are the maximum and minimum [major radii](name:major_radius) on its poloidal contour. These coordinates refer to the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The extrema are taken over the entire [radial outline of the plasma boundary](name:radial_outline_of_plasma_boundary), whose total major-radius span is twice this minor radius. This is a single contour-wide size parameter, not a local major-radius coordinate, a flux-surface average, or the distance from the magnetic axis to an individual boundary point. No circular-cross-section assumption is implied.

The last closed magnetic flux surface: the outermost flux surface on which field lines close on themselves, bounding the confined plasma. Where $\psi = \psi_{\mathrm{LCFS}}$, $\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux; $\psi_{\mathrm{LCFS}}$ is its value on the last closed flux surface.

definition: Poloidal arc length of a closed magnetic-flux-surface contour in an equilibrium poloidal cross-section, measuring the perimeter of that selected surface. At each equilibrium time slice, this scalar is obtained in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius, φ is toroidal angle, and Z is vertical height, by integrating sqrt((dR/dθ)^2 + (dZ/dθ)^2) dθ at fixed φ over one complete circuit, with θ any smooth contour parameter and its integration endpoints representing the same contour point. It includes no averaging or summation over multiple surfaces and is expressed in m.
documentation:
The poloidal length is the perimeter of the closed contour formed by one selected magnetic flux surface in a poloidal cross-section. It is a geometric property of the surface boundary, rather than its enclosed area, volume, or toroidal circumference.

The contour length is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height:

$$
L_{\mathrm{pol}} = \int_{\theta_a}^{\theta_b} \sqrt{\left(\frac{dR(\theta)}{d\theta}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{dZ(\theta)}{d\theta}\right)^2}\,d\theta
$$

Here $L_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the poloidal length, $\theta$ is any smooth parameter along the contour, $R(\theta)$ and $Z(\theta)$ are its cylindrical coordinate functions, and $\theta_a$ and $\theta_b$ are parameter values at the same contour point after one complete circuit. The contour is taken at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$.

The quantity applies to one magnetic flux surface and includes the complete closed poloidal contour, with no averaging or summation over multiple surfaces. It excludes local arc segments and geometric quantities associated with the enclosed region. The selected surface may be labeled by the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate).

Unlike [elongation of a flux surface](name:elongation_of_flux_surface), which describes a scale-independent cross-sectional shape ratio, the poloidal length retains the absolute geometric scale of the contour.

definition: Whole-plasma toroidal beta rescaled by plasma size, reference toroidal magnetic field and plasma current: beta_N = 100 * beta_tor * a[m] * B0[T] / Ip[MA], where beta_N is normalized toroidal beta, beta_tor is the dimensionless ratio of volume-averaged total perpendicular plasma pressure to the reference toroidal magnetic pressure, a is plasma minor radius in metres, B0 is the reference vacuum toroidal magnetic field in tesla, and Ip is net toroidal plasma current in megaamperes. The numerical-unit convention and factor of 100 are part of the definition; the result has unit 1. The signed ratio B0/Ip is retained. Pressure may be determined by equilibrium reconstruction. Unlike normalized toroidal thermal beta, the pressure input is not restricted to thermal pressure.
documentation: This global plasma parameter expresses toroidal pressure loading after the conventional current-and-geometry rescaling used in MHD stability and confinement assessment. It differs from toroidal beta by the explicit factor of 100 and the minor-radius, reference-field and inverse-current factors, so retaining “normalized” distinguishes a separate quantity rather than an optional reporting convention. Total pressure includes the represented thermal and nonthermal contributions; using pressure from equilibrium reconstruction changes the pressure estimate, not the normalization. Restricting the input to thermal pressure instead gives normalized toroidal thermal beta. The normalization assumes positive minor radius and nonzero reference field and plasma current, without replacing the signed field or current by its magnitude.
